The character for "Māra" (魔) has been understood since the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty as one who can afflict people, hence it was changed to "ghost" (鬼). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Most of these are 'un-thought' (不思爾). A Bodhisattva of Liberation should manifest as a Māra-king.

On the sixth heaven above, there is a separate residence for Māras, which is subsumed under the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*); this refers to the "Māra of the Devaputra. Prior to this, they were collectively termed the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*). [In the commentary on] the rules, "desire" refers to food, drink, sleep, and sexual desire. Furthermore, a verse says: "The six ways of receiving desire: embracing, holding hands, laughing, and gazing.

Sexual desire ranges from the Four Heavenly Kings to the Trāyastriṃśa (embracing), Yāma (holding hands), Tuṣita (laughing), Nirmāṇarati (gazing intently), and Paranirmita-vaśavartin (glancing briefly). There are varying degrees of thickness in the existence of desire. It is also called... [text breaks off].

The Realm of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies (the heavens, humans, and the three miserable paths; asuras are subsumed under the heavenly destiny, while ghosts and animals pervade all five destinies—all possess the three types of desire). Second, the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*):

although they are free from the defilement of desire, they still possess material substance, and are thus called the Form Realm. They are collectively termed the Brahma-worlds because they have already abandoned the defilement of desire.
They are generally designated as the Four Dhyānas because they are free from agitation and movement. Birth in this realm is induced solely by the ten wholesome actions of the Desire Realm.

The heavens are produced through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), yet these are merely the sixfold practice of impure (*sāsrava*) dhyāna-contemplation. (The six practices consist of: revulsion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstruction of the desire realm;
and aspiration for the purity, excellence, and detachment of the form realm. This is the mundane path of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) that suppresses afflictions and transcends the world.

Regarding the first dhyāna, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* calls it the "ground of joy and bliss born of seclusion" (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*), meaning that by being secluded from the mixed evils of the desire realm, one attains the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). Regarding the second dhyāna... [the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* calls it]...

The second dhyāna is called the stage of joy and bliss born of concentration; it means that the water of concentration moistens the karma, so that mental anxiety does not oppress one. (Zizhong says: From the second dhyāna upward, there is no verbal expression;
rather, the light is emitted by the concentrated mind, and its superior or inferior quality distinguishes its high or low level. The third dhyāna is called the stage of wondrous bliss apart from joy;

although the mind is separated from joy, joy and bliss are inherently present. (The *Chumen* states: The first dhyāna has five factors: applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; the second dhyāna has four factors: internal purity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.)

The third dhyāna has five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind (the characteristics of its cultivation and realization are detailed within the section on śamatha and vipaśyanā).

The fourth dhyāna has nine natural heavens; as for the retributive realms of the fourth dhyāna, there are only three heavens, while the Āsaṃjñika-sattva heaven is separately established from the Bṛhatphala heaven. According to the sūtras, there are two paths: one proceeds directly to the Bṛhatphala heaven, while the other takes a circuitous route to the Āsaṃjñika-sattva heaven.

Above these four [dhyānas] are the five Anāgāmin heavens (so called because they no longer take birth in the desire realm); these are the distinct meditative concentrations cultivated by noble ones to augment their spiritual resources.

Because they are the fruit of karma and differ from those of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), they are listed separately; they are also called the Five Pure Abodes (*pañca śuddhāvāsāḥ*). Their general name is the Ground of Purity of Equanimity and Mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi-bhūmi*).

(The *Chumen* states: "The four dhyānas have four factors: neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind. They are also called the Four Fundamental Dhyānas (*mūla-catur-dhyāna*). (The *Chumen* states:

"The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transformations, and the wisdom of untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā-prajñā*)—all various dhyānas and samādhis emerge from these; therefore, they are called 'fundamental. [The third is] the Three... [text ends].
In the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are four heavens where the matter resulting from karma does not exist, but the matter resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi-phala-rūpa*) does;

this applies equally to both the environment and the inhabitants. Here, one extinguishes the body and returns to the nature of formlessness. These are the abodes of Śrāvakas, or the distinct retributions of non-Buddhist practitioners of the Non-Perception realm (*asaṃjñika*), or gods who have abandoned and loathed [sensual desire];

their types are manifold, yet all lack the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). (From the Form Realm up to this point, according to the interpretation of Wēnlíng. As for the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it is that which the practitioner loathes...

If one is troubled by the fact that form (rūpa) ensnares the mind and desires liberation from it, one should immediately cultivate the wisdom of insight (vipaśyanā-jñāna) to destroy the three kinds of form: (1) visible and resistant form, which refers to the visual object-field perceived by the eye;

(2) invisible and resistant form, which refers to sound, odor, taste, and touch; and (3) invisible and non-resistant form, which refers to the mental object-field (dharmāyatana) conditioned by the mind, namely, non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa).

As for the station of consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), it means that having become weary of and averse to infinite space, one cultivates insight and relinquishes the previous external emptiness to further take internal consciousness as the object. As for the station of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), [it refers to] the external...
The object is called "emptiness," and the internal object is called "consciousness. Abandoning these two objects, one enters the concentration of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

As for those who enter the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they abandon the perception of the sphere of consciousness—which is not non-perception—and the non-perception of the sphere of nothingness—which is not perception—and enter the higher concentration.

(The first gate also states: "Ordinary people and non-Buddhists attain this concentration, claiming it is the realization of *nirvāṇa* and the severance of all perception; therefore, they say there is 'neither perception. However, the disciples of the Buddha know according to reality that subtle [perception] still exists.")

Because they dwell relying upon the fourfold assembly, it is said that they are not without conceptualization (asaṃjñin); thus, the attainment and loss [of this state] are combined into a single name. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"All the celestial hosts employ noble speech; their language is identical to that of Central India, yet it is not through study that they understand their own scriptures and words."
Regarding the discussion on the body (*kāya*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are two meanings. First, concerning "having no place" (*asthāna*):

the *Vaibhāṣika* school states that the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*) are free from physical retribution and have no distinct location; rather, one accomplishes the karma for the four formless realms while abiding within the desire and form realms.

Regarding "having no body" (*akāya*): the *Abhidharmakośa* states that the formless realm has no body. The *Zuǎn* (Compendium) explains: "There is no matter of karmic fruit (*karmaphala-rūpa*); it is not a body of maturation (*vipākakāya*)."

Yan says that in the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the body and mind are extinguished, and the nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) manifests; there is no matter produced by karma (*karmaja-rūpa*). (The Gushan commentary notes:

"The absence of matter produced by karma indicates the presence of matter produced by concentration. Next, regarding the phrase "there are locations," the *Lokadhātunirdeśa* states that beyond the Akaniṣṭha heaven, there are the space-realm (*ākāśāyatana*) and so forth, up to the Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception realm (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), all of which are called dwelling places of the devas.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that the olfactory faculty of a Bodhisattva perceives...
Regarding the fragrance of the palaces of the formless realm, it is said that those who possess a body [are affected].

The *Āgama* states: "When Śāriputra passed away, the devas of the formless realm shed tears like a fine spring rain. The *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* lists them among the assemblies of the formless realm devas. The *Gandharva-madhyamāntara-bhava Sūtra* states:

"The Tathāgata went to the formless realm, where the various devas prostrated to him. The Mahāsāṃghika school says: "It is simply that they lack coarse form; it is not that they are entirely non-existent."

Regarding "subtle matter" (*sūkṣmarūpa*), the *Jingming jing shu* (Commentary on the Śrīmālā-sūtra) states: "If one follows the teachings of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), it is explained that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is without matter;

if one follows the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it is explained that the formless realm possesses matter. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The matter of the formless realm is not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
What is clarified here should follow the latter sense.
Discourse on the Lords of Devas:

There are two senses in which the lords of devas are discussed—the general and the specific. Regarding the general sense, Māra, Brahmā, and those of the Desire and Form Realms each have their presiding lord. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states:

"The Four Heavenly Kings preside over the four continents" (this refers to their acting as lords by traveling about to bestow rewards and met out punishments). The *Dazhidu Lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states that Śakra is the lord of the two [realms].

The Lord of the Heavens (the Four Kings and Trāyastriṃśa) is the ruler of the Desire Realm (because he dwells at the summit of the Desire Realm). The Great Brahmā King is the ruler of the Three Realms.
According to the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), Śakra is the Lord of the Earth-dwelling heavens, while Brahmā is the Lord of the Sahā World;

they govern the great trichiliocosm (governing both above and below). In the *Tianren gantong zhuan* (Biographies of the Resonance between Heaven and Humans), it is answered that although the Māra King is the ruler of the Desire Realm...
If Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings practice the Buddha-dharma, Māra cannot restrain them. The Cloud of Sublime Joy (Māradhvaja) is the lord of form (*rūpa*) and also the lord of the three realms;
Māra is the lord of desire. Regarding the commentary on the *Xiuxing* [Bodhisattva-bhūmi]: "The Brahmā King is the lord of the three realms, while all others are his subjects.
According to another treatise, there are three points: first, discussing the Brahmā King alone, the text states: "The Brahmā King dwells in the intermediate stage of the First Dhyāna."
Internally there is vitarka and vicāra, and externally there is speech; one who attains mastery over these becomes a king. Cultivating dhyāna alone makes one a Brahmā-minister (brahmapurohita);

adding the four immeasurable minds (apramāṇa-citta) makes one a Brahmā-king (brahmā-rāja). Furthermore, it is said that the title "Brahmā-king" signifies commanding those above and crowning those below.
According to the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, because there is no method of verbal expression from the second dhyāna upward, [the Brahmā-king] does not exist there.
The *Lìwáng Chánmén* states: "In the first dhyāna, because there is a mind of vitarka and vicāra, there is the dharma of speech;

it is for the sake of convenience that [the deity] presides over the sentient beings of the lower stages. Furthermore, the *Dúlùn Móhē Dàlùn* states: "Maheśvara has eight arms and three eyes and rides a white ox. It further states:
"Beyond the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, there are Bodhisattvas of the ten abodes known as Mahāmaheśvara, who [govern] a trichiliocosm."
The *Kṣitigarbha-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states: "The Lord of the World, Maheśvara. The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says:
"The Lord of the Great Trichiliocosm, Maheśvara. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "If one says the Lord of the World is precisely Maheśvara.
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says: "Maheśvara can cover the great trichiliocosm; taking the World-Honored One as the basis for transformation, he stands in opposition to the three Māras and Brahmā."
The *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and presides over the trichiliocosm (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*).
If the *Lotus Sūtra* lists Brahmā, the King of the World, as the lord of the world, he actually governs only a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍikālokadhātu*);

it is merely because the scribe praises him that he is called 'lord. I privately maintain that Zhan’an’s judgment—that this [Maheśvara] is one who has attained the status of being the lord within the trichiliocosm—is correct."
The Lord descends here because within this Great Trichiliocosm there are ten billion Brahmā kings;

since the Brahmā king Śikhin resides in the center of this Great Trichiliocosm, he is designated as the "Lord. As for the other Brahmās, their respective abodes are partial, and thus they cannot be called lords.
Therefore, it is now determined that Maheśvara resides at the Peak of Form (Bhavāgra) and is the lord of the Brahmā kings by virtue of his superior retribution.
Dwelling within the great trichiliocosm, one takes sovereign governance as the primary task.
Regarding the four dhyānas and four stages (*bhūmi*),

it is said that from antiquity until now, those who discourse on the heavens have not understood the meaning of the four dhyānas and four stages, because the various texts are arranged in such a dense array.

One cannot distinguish [the locations] based on the ear; according to the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-śruti-skandha*, the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, and other texts, the heavens are arranged in vertical succession, each separated by a distance that doubles the preceding one, and all possess their own dwelling grounds (*sthāna-bhūmi*). These established doctrines are not sufficient to rely upon.
Now, following the *Abhidharmakośa*, it is said that the Brahmā Heaven has no separate location, but rather possesses a high tower within the Brahmā-purohita Heaven.
The same applies to this Dharma Garden: Mahābrahmā is the sovereign, the Brahmapurohitas are the ministers, and the Brahmakāyikas are the subjects.

According to this, the three heavens are all situated together in the First Dhyāna on a single level. If the Sāṃmitīya school maintains that the Unconscious Beings (Asaṃjñisattvas) and the Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) dwell in one place because their bodies, lifespans, and merits do not differ, the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states that from the Heaven of Merit-Love (Puṇyaprasava), there are two diverging paths.

The realm where merit and virtue are perfectly bright is called the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala); the realm where body and mind are extinguished is called the Heaven of No-Thought (Asaṃjñisattva). (These two branches merely divide into two categories;

they are identical in meaning to the Sāṃkhya school and occupy the same location. It is further said that within this there are five more heavens of Non-returners (Anāgāmin)—referring here to the fourth dhyāna.

The celestial kings of the four stages of the fourth dhyāna possess only a reverent hearing [of the Dharma] but cannot know or see it, just as those in deep mountain retreats or at places of practice (ārāma) in the mundane world.
Arhats dwell in the world, yet they cannot be seen by coarse people; based on this, we know that only one among the Bṛhatphala gods is called "King.
Within this [realm], five types of Anāgāmins and one non-Buddhist practitioner coexist, for the fourth dhyāna consists of only a single stage.
The *Cidi Chanmen* (Successive Dhyāna Gate) states: "The Buddha spoke of the eighteen Brahmās in the *Renwang Jing*; there must also be a sovereign among them."

Furthermore, it is said that within the four *dhyānas* there are Great Tranquil Kings (*mahāśāntirāja*). The *Sūtra on the Garland of Brahmā-kings* clarifies that each *dhyāna* has its own Brahmā-king.
The *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra* also identifies four kings for the four stages of the four *dhyānas*.

In the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, among the thirty-nine positions listed in the assembly, those in the desire realm heavens are titled "kings," while in the form realm, each *dhyāna* is titled "king"; other heavens are not so listed. Now, let us examine this in detail.

Since Dhyāna takes Mahābrahmā as its sovereign, and all three sūtras (the *Ratnarāśi*, the *Śrīmālādevī*, and the *Śūraṅgama*) state that the four dhyānas each have a sovereign, we know that the three heavens of Ābhāsvara, Śubhakṛtsna, and Bṛhatphala are all sovereigns, while all others follow the principle of being merely ministers or subjects.
Therefore, following the intent of the *Mahāyānaprasādaprabhāvana-sūtra*, the first through fourth dhyānas are established as four stages; thus, [the third stage] is called "Bṛhatphala."

The King of Happiness (Sukhāvatī), the Cloudless (Anabhraka), the Ministers (Puṇyaprasava), the Five Non-returners (Pañca-anāgāmin), and one non-Buddhist (tīrthika) inhabit the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala).
These nine heavens above are all co-located within the single stage of the Fourth Dhyāna (as the Second and Third Dhyānas are to be understood by analogy).

Alternatively, because the lifespans of the various heavenly bodies differ, they must each occupy distinct locations, as is the case in various Sūtras and Śāstras concerning the Lesser Vehicle; such is the position of the Brahmā Kings.
Furthermore, as for the Brahmapurohitas and the Brahmakāyikas, their bodies and lifespans are all of unequal length;

likewise, although those in the Bṛhatphala and the Asaṃjñisattvas [live] for five hundred kalpas, among the Bṛhatphala there are those who die prematurely, whereas the retribution of the asaṃjñi-samāpatti is fully completed.

Judging by this, although their bodies and lifespans differ, it does not hinder them from dwelling in the same place, just as among the people of Jambudvīpa there are those who live long and those who die young. Moreover—
Regarding the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra’s statement that all the celestial kings are bodhisattvas of the tenth stage: these are all provisional manifestations who come to lead those at the level of reality.
Among the heavens, they transform those beings who possess the retribution of the heavens, causing them to seek liberation from karmic conditions within the heavens; thus they may be called "kings.
If one were to claim that a king dwells in a remote place, isolated and distinct from the other devas, then what purpose would such a king serve for the other devas?
On what basis could one refrain from composing this treatise? Would that not greatly contradict its intended meaning?
Or, as the *Abhidharma* suggests, if it is said that there is no method of verbal expression above the Second Dhyāna, how then can there be transformation [through teaching]?

However, since the Ābhāsvara gods already use light as their speech, we know that for the various devas of the higher realms, every movement and gesture is nothing other than verbal instruction. Inferring from this principle, there is nothing that is not possible.

Regarding the question in the *Vaibhāṣa-śāstra* concerning the thirty-two heavens—namely, the six heavens of desire (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu*), the eighteen Brahma-heavens (*aṣṭādaśa-brahma-loka*), the four formless heavens (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), as well as the [heavens of] the *Gandharvas*, *Kinnaras*, *Cūḍapanthakas*, and *Mālādharas*, along with the sun, moon, and constellations: how many are inhabited by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and how many by noble ones (*ārya*)?
Answer: Two are inhabited exclusively by ordinary beings; five are inhabited exclusively by noble ones; and the remaining twenty-five heavens are inhabited by both ordinary beings and noble ones.
Regarding the two types of abodes mentioned, one is the Great Brahmā King of the First Dhyāna. Failing to understand the causes of karma, he claims only that "I am the creator of heaven and earth.
Relying on this, he becomes arrogant and treats all others with contempt; therefore, the Sage does not dwell together with him.
Furthermore, among those in the Heaven of Non-conception, there are only non-Buddhists who have cultivated the non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) to be born therein.
Having received the retribution for five hundred kalpas of mindlessness, those outside the Way (tīrthikas), failing to understand it, claim it is nirvāṇa.
Once this retribution is exhausted, they will inevitably give rise to false views and be reborn in hell; even sages are not born there.

As for the "five exclusively inhabited by sages," these are the five Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa)—such as the Heaven of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) and above, including the Heaven Free from Affliction (Avṛha) and the Heaven Free from Heat (Atapa)—which are inhabited exclusively by non-returners (anāgāmin) and arhats.

This is the place where they dwell. Generally speaking, those who are born in that heaven must be those who are progressing toward the stage of Anāgāmin (Non-returner), who have attained the four *dhyānas*, and who have given rise to untainted (*anāsrava*) states and initiated the karma of perfumed meditation (*vāsana-dhyāna*).
Only after initiating one grade up to nine grades of this karma can they be born there.

Because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack this karma of perfumed meditation, they cannot be born there. If one were to say that it is logically possible for an Anāgāmin to be born there, that would not be the case.
Question: Since an Arhat is already one who is not subject to rebirth (*anupapatti*), why is it also said that they are born in those heavens? Answer:

This should be explained as follows: it is a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) of the desire realm who is born there and attains Arhatship; it does not mean that they were already an Arhat prior to being born there.
The three realms, taken both collectively and individually, are collectively termed the *kāmadhātu*, *rūpadhātu*, and *ārūpyadhātu*.

From the base level at the Diamond Throne (*vajrāsana*) up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), within which the five destinies (*gati*) dwell intermingled, all sentient beings have not yet abandoned desire; therefore, it is called the *kāmadhātu*. From this point upward...
From the Brahmakāyika heaven up to Akaniṣṭha, these eighteen heavens constitute the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu).

Because the physical forms of the primary retribution bodies and their palaces are like silver-white in color, and because the light of the colors of true gold and red mutually illuminate one another, they are called the "Form Realm.

From the Sphere of Infinite Space up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, the celestial beings of these four levels share the same realm as the azure void. Since they form bodies from the four aggregates excluding the aggregate of form, they are called the "Formless Realm" (Arūpyadhātu).
The Formless Realm (also known as the Three Existences) has twenty-five distinct names for its "existences" (*bhava*):

namely, the four continents, the four evil destinies (hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and *asuras*), the six heavens of the desire realm together with the Brahma heavens, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and the five non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
These are all called "existences" because their causes belong to the outflows (*āsrava*), their fruits are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and they involve birth and death.
The *Sūtra on the Causes and Effects of the Five Signs of Decline* states: "The bodies of devas and humans are pure and do not receive dust or grime;

they possess great radiance, their minds are constantly joyful, and there is nothing that does not accord with their wishes. Yet, even they are oppressed by the fire of desire. When their merit is exhausted, the five signs of decline appear."

First, the flowers upon their heads wither; second, their eyes blink; third, the radiance of their bodies fades; fourth, sweat breaks out from their armpits; fifth, they spontaneously depart from their original seats.

(According to the *Mahīśāsaka*, there is also the defilement of their clothing and the production of a foul odor from their bodies; the absence of blinking, the fading of radiance, and the remaining three signs are the same as above.

Furthermore, it is said that these sons of gods, having originally cultivated a small amount of merit to receive the retribution of celestial bliss, will experience great suffering when that retribution is about to end.

Affliction is the root from which one falls into the three evil realms; though one originally performs wholesome deeds in pursuit of pleasant retribution, one now obtains little pleasure and subsequently encounters much suffering.
It is like a hungry person eating food mixed with poison: although it is delicious at first, it ultimately results in great calamity. How could a wise person crave such pleasure?
When the gods of the form and formless realms see that their lifespans are long, they claim it is eternal bliss; yet once they see—
When transformation and decay give rise to great suffering and affliction, one immediately conceives false views and slanders the existence of cause and effect;

for this reason, one cycles through the three miserable realms and undergoes all manner of suffering, such that not a single joy exists within the three worlds. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When a Bodhisattva attains the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), he perceives the blissful meditative states of the gods in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
yet, his mind becomes attached to them, and he does not realize that his life has ended, causing him to fall back into the desire realm."
Within the realms, beings take on the forms and colors of birds and beasts; it is likewise for the various devas who fall from their pure abodes and again undergo sexual desire amidst impurity.

The six heavens of the Desire Realm, being attached to the five desires, fall back into the hells—just as Udraka Rāmaputra, after the exhaustion of the retribution for attaining the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, fell into the body of a flying fox.

The commentary states: Now, the three realms are established in their fixed positions and the six paths of existence are divided; their appearances differ in coarseness and subtlety, and their traces diverge in suffering and joy.
When one contemplates their origin, they do not transcend form and mind; when one examines where they ultimately converge, they are nothing other than arising and ceasing.

This cycle of arising and ceasing is what is called impermanence. Form and mind are illusory shadows, serving as the very root of suffering; therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* characterizes them with the analogy of a great river.

The Flowering Region (China) is like a burning house; the Sage awakens us to leave this chariot behind and return to the source, transcending the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and gradually perfecting the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

Consider this: although celestial retribution may be abundant and magnificent, with garments and ornaments ever-new and the physical form light and subtle, even such sovereignty in the heavens is merely the realm of the Māra-kings.

Within the state of non-conceptual absorption (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), one becomes a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*); following the attainment of the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it turns into a false concentration.

I have once again fallen into the body of a wildcat; the defilements of the six desire realms and my delusions are so profound that I am unable to uphold the Prajñāpāramitā or make offerings to Nirvāṇa.
My arrogance increases further, and my notions of self and personhood become ever more superior.

Consequently, my head has suddenly withered, sweat flows from my armpits, the radiance of my jeweled palace has faded, and my fine silken robes are now covered in grime. When merit is exhausted and decline arrives, it is difficult to escape impermanence; relying upon this pure mind, [I repent].
May all be completely purified through repentance; may all universally vow to forever leave behind the causes of suffering and ascend to the eternal bliss of the Pure Land.
The mind gives rise to the diagrams of the six realms;
every person possesses a mind, and where there is a mind, there must be thoughts. When thoughts arise, they are inevitably either defiled or pure. "Defiled" refers to grasping and attachment.
The purification of the six sense objects means not grasping at them. Furthermore, among worldly people, there are none who do not become defiled by the six sense objects.
If one grasps at the six sense objects and gives rise to karma such as greed, anger, lust, and killing, this is evil.

If one does not give rise to greed, anger, lust, killing, and so forth toward the six sense objects, this is good. Moreover, to practice giving, precepts, patience, and so forth regarding the six sense objects is [also good].
The karmic actions of good and evil are completed in the present, and their retributions of suffering and joy respond in the future.

Because there are differences of superior, middling, and inferior within the causes—goodness and evil—their fruits differ in terms of ascent or descent, manifesting as the realms of devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Within these six destinies, one continues to create karma, and karma in turn continues to produce retribution.
Therefore, the cycle of the six realms of rebirth does not cease; observing its origin, one sees it arises from the thoughts of my own mind.
Thus the Buddha said: "The three realms are but mind; all phenomena are but consciousness. For this reason, those who cultivate the Way well must clarify this point alone:

they must be cautious regarding their initial thoughts and restrain their defiled minds—this is the essential method. If one does not grasp at the six sense objects, then by not grasping, [one attains liberation].

Without karma, there is no karma; thus, there is no retribution. Therefore, when not a single thought arises, the six realms of existence are simultaneously dissolved and the cycle of saṃsāra is severed.

Once the seeds of karma are cut off, one departs from the triple world. If one abides in non-arising and realizes the true body and mind, such that they are forever at rest, this constitutes the two vehicles.
If, from the state of non-arising, one gives rise to the six perfections and the myriad practices, this constitutes Bodhi.

If a Mahāyāna practitioner merely appears to have severed [afflictions]—yet has not truly severed the root of afflictions, has not realized [the truth], and still harbors heterodox views and false attachments—they are a follower of external paths (tīrthika) who has not yet escaped saṃsāra.
Therefore, bondage and liberation depend on the gaining or losing of the mind; let the practitioner examine this with discernment.

The Calculation of Kalpas and Years (Although previously we have observed the three realms, we have only explained their vertical height and have not yet reached their breadth; therefore, next we explain the Great Trichiliocosm so that one may fully know the infinite triple worlds in all eight directions and exhaustively understand the vastness of the Buddha-fields).
Regarding the diagram of the thousandfold world system and the exposition of the Great Trichiliocosm,
the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The great earth of the trichiliocosm is formed through immeasurable causes and conditions, serving as its support."
The water-circle rests upon the wind-circle; the wind rests upon space; space has no support. The world abides through the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* states: "Because the Buddhas have accomplished inconceivable wisdom, they are able to know the characteristics of all winds and rains.
They know that there is a great wind named Ulūpaka, which causes sentient beings to experience various sensations."
All are moved and shaken by this wind. This wind-wheel is three *krośas* high (a *krośa*, here translated as "the distance of one drum-beat," is five *li* in the *Miśrakābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*).
Above this wind, within the void of space, there is another wind-wheel named *Cāmara*.
The measurement of this wind-wheel is ten *yojanas* high. In this manner, one can fully comprehend the characteristics of the eight thousand successive wind-wheels.
One should know that the supreme wind-circle, named "Pervading the Upper Realms," serves as the support for the water-circle;
the height of this water is eight hundred thousand yojanas, serving as the support for the great earth.
The height of this earth is sixty-eight thousand yojanas. Upon the surface of this earth lies a trichiliocosm. (From the *Dīrgha Āgama*).
It is said that the sun and moon travel around the four continents, and the area illuminated by their light constitutes one world-system (*lokadhātu*).
Within such a thousandfold world-system, there are a thousand suns and moons, a thousand Sumeru Kings of Mountains, four thousand sets of four continents, four thousand great oceans,
four thousand evil realms, a thousand kings of Yama, a thousand sets of Four Heavenly Kings, and a thousand Trāyastriṃśa heavens up to a thousand Brahmā worlds.
A thousand such heavens as these constitute a small chiliocosm; a thousand such small chiliocosms constitute a medium chiliocosm;
and a thousand such medium chiliocosms constitute a great trichiliocosm.

Within each of these, there are ten billion Sumeru mountains, four continents, suns and moons, up to the Brahma heavens; collectively, these are termed a single Buddha-field. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Four..."

The four continents, the sun and moon, Mount Meru, the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the Brahma worlds—each one thousand of these constitutes what is called a "small chiliocosm" (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*).

A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a "medium chiliocosm" (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*). A thousand times this medium chiliocosm is called a "great trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*).

All of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously. (The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, and the *Prakaraṇāryavāca-śāstra* all agree on the enumeration of the great trichiliocosm as stated above. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "These... [text continues].

When the King of Men held up an incense burner to make offerings during the recitation of the sutra, its fragrance spread throughout the trichiliocosm in a single thought-moment, reaching as far as ten billion suns and moons and even ten billion heavens of the Non-Perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One emitted ten billion rays of light from the wheels beneath his two feet, illuminating this trichiliocosm."

Within a great trichiliocosm—consisting of ten billion sets of four continents, ten billion great oceans, ten billion Cakravāḍa mountains, ten billion Sumeru mountains, the six heavens of the desire realm, and so forth up to ten billion Akaniṣṭha heavens—all that exists therein is clearly manifested. The *Huayan Chao* states:
"If one speaks of a small chiliocosm, one counts only the first dhyāna; if one counts a medium chiliocosm, one counts the second dhyāna. This is because the second [dhyāna]...

Because the extent of the first dhyāna is equal to a medium chiliocosm, whereas if one were to calculate the extent of a great trichiliocosm, it would correspond to three dhyānas; this is because the extent of the third dhyāna is equal to a great trichiliocosm.
Thus, we know that within a great trichiliocosm there are ten billion first-dhyāna realms, one million second-dhyāna realms, one thousand third-dhyāna realms, and only one fourth-dhyāna realm.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The extent of the first dhyāna is as vast as the four continents; the second dhyāna is like a small..."

One thousand second dhyānas are equal to a middle chiliocosm, and one thousand fourth dhyānas are equal to a great trichiliocosm (according to this, the previous note should state that the measure of the second dhyāna is equal to a small chiliocosm and the measure of the third dhyāna is equal to a middle chiliocosm;
this is correct). ○ The Commentary states: The sacred words of the Buddha ought logically to be non-contradictory. Why, then, do the sūtras and śāstras differ from one another?
Regarding the number of Sumeru mountains, if one follows the *Āgamas*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and other texts, there are ten billion Sumerus within a great trichiliocosm.
In the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and other sutras, there are ten billion Sumerus; thus, their numbers differ.

Furthermore, some say that within a trichiliocosm there are ten billion fourth-dhyāna heavens, which makes their extent the most narrow; others say there is only one fourth-dhyāna heaven, which makes its extent the most vast.
Thus, there is this difference in their breadth and narrowness. Moreover, some say there are four formless heavens (*ārūpyadhātu*), while others say there are none.
"O Deva, why is there this difference in increase and decrease? He replied: "Although there are slight differences, each has its own principle.
To illustrate the numbers of one assembly: first, a small chiliocosm is like one string of coins (one coin being like one Sumeru mountain, and one thousand coins being like one thousand Sumerus);
a medium chiliocosm is like one thousand strings of coins; and a great trichiliocosm is like one million strings of coins. Though they are counted in this way..."
The various scales of magnitude do not exceed these thousands of thousands; for what reason? It is because there are four levels of the term "koṭi" (hundred million).

If one hundred thousand is taken as a koṭi, then a great trichiliocosm contains ten trillion Sumeru mountains. If one million is taken as a koṭi, then a great trichiliocosm contains one trillion Sumeru mountains.
If ten million is taken as a koṭi, then a great trichiliocosm contains one hundred billion Sumeru mountains. If...

If ten million is reckoned as one hundred million (*koṭi*), then a great trichiliocosm contains ten billion Sumeru mountains. By applying this principle, whether one counts by hundreds or by tens of thousands, it is all permissible;
in total, nothing exceeds the realm of this great trichiliocosm. Regarding the relative breadth and narrowness of the second assembly:
for instance, the measure of the second dhyāna is equal to a small chiliocosm; if one takes a small chiliocosm from the first dhyāna upward, there are one thousand such worlds.
In the second dhyāna there are likewise ten billion first dhyānas; taking it further upward, there are ten billion fourth dhyānas.
It is like summer clouds covering the nine provinces: if one takes them by province, there are nine clouds; if one takes them by commandery, there are over four hundred clouds;
if one takes them by county, the number reaches the thousands and is not small. Some say that a single cloud covers the myriad nations.

It is said that each of the ten thousand nations has its own "summer clouds," which can be perceived through contemplation. Regarding the increase and decrease of the three heavens, there are two interpretations:

if one follows the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and other such texts, there are four heavens of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) above the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); however, if one follows the *Avataṃsaka*, these are restricted to specific locations only up to the summit of the realm of form.
Yet, when considering the dharmas of the ground, they pervade the four heavens of emptiness; since the heavens of emptiness have no fixed location, they are present wherever one is.
Attaining the fruit is like attaining the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); one experiences the retribution of the fruit right there in the desire realm.
Therefore, there is no separate location, as it is subsumed within these two realms. The *Abhidharma* states:
"From this edge of the summit of Mount Sumeru to that edge of the summit of Mount Sumeru is twelve billion, three hundred and forty-five *yojana*s; from the center of this Mount Sumeru..."
The distance from the center of this mountain to the center of that mountain is twelve hundred and eight million three thousand four hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
From the base of this mountain to the base of that mountain is twelve hundred and three thousand fifteen *yojanas*.
The distances between the mountains in the eight directions are likewise the same. This is what the Buddha has taught. Some say that outside of the thousand *Sumerus* there is one small [Sumeru].
Outside the Cakravāḍa Mountains, they encircle [the world] up to the height of the First Dhyāna;
outside the intermediate chiliocosm, there is a middle Cakravāḍa Mountain that encircles it up to the height of the Second Dhyāna;

and outside the great trichiliocosm, there is a great Cakravāḍa Mountain that encircles it up to the height of the Third Dhyāna (furthermore, outside each Sumeru and its four continents, there is one small Cakravāḍa Mountain, making four such sets in total). Within the great Cakravāḍa Mountains, all that is encompassed extends upward to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Imagine that from the lowest limit, the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), all are collectively termed a "trichiliocosm" (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). Because it is accumulated through three stages, it is called "three thousand.
By omitting the "small" and "medium" [units] and citing only the final one, it is called a "great thousand. When this great trichiliocosm is formed, it forms simultaneously;
when it perishes, it perishes simultaneously. It is universally designated as the *Sāha* world, which is the realm for the conversion and guidance of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
Also: A Diagram of the Great Trichiliocosm Encompassing Dhyāna;
A Diagram of the Increasing Numerical Values of the Great Trichiliocosm.
One world (the area illuminated by one sun and moon); ○ (this is according to the additive system of calculation used by the Yellow Emperor);
ten worlds (ten suns and moons); ten; hundred worlds (a hundred suns and moons); hundred (ten tens).
Small chiliocosm (one small chiliocosm); thousand (ten hundred);
ten thousand worlds (ten small chiliocosms); ten thousand (ten thousand); [the number "hundred million" has four levels, etc.];
hundred thousand worlds (a hundred small chiliocosms); hundred million (one million); ○ (this hundred-millionfold great trichiliocosm contains ten billion Mount Sumerus).

Middle Thousand (a thousand small thousands constitute one middle thousand); *zhào* (one billion or also one million); ○ (this constitutes a billion great thousands [of worlds], with ten billion Mount Sumerus);
Ten Thousand Thousands (ten middle thousands); *jīng* (ten *zhào*, or also ten million); ○ (this constitutes a billion great thousands [of worlds], with ten billion Mount Sumerus);

Hundred Thousand Thousands (a hundred middle thousands); *hài* (ten *jīng*, or also ten thousand times ten thousand); ○ (this constitutes a billion great thousands [of worlds], with ten billion Mount Sumerus).
A trichiliocosm (the great thousandfold world system, consisting of a thousand times a thousand middling worlds); a koṭi (ten *hāyas*, also meaning ten million);
and *kalpa*—the term "kalpa" is a general designation for a vast duration of time. In Sanskrit, it is fully called *kalpavarta* (abbreviated as *kalpa*). This...
It is said that a *mahā-kalpa* (great aeon) is exceedingly vast and cannot be calculated by years or months;
therefore, the Sages provisionally employ metaphors such as the rubbing of a stone, a mustard seed, a city, or the limits of the formation and destruction of fire and water to indicate its duration.

There are many kinds of *kalpas*, but briefly speaking, they are the great and small aeons of formation and destruction. First, regarding the four types of *antarakalpa* (intermediate aeons), there is one [type] of increasing...

[Subtracting] two *kalpas* of formation (*vivartakalpa*) and forty [of each of the other three]—which combine the period of abiding (*sthāpana*) with formation; thirty *kalpas* of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*) and forty [of each of the other three]—which combine the period of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) with destruction;

and four great *kalpas* (the total of formation and destruction, excluding the individual *kalpas*). If these are further expanded, there are six *kalpas*: first, the individual; second, formation; third, abiding; fourth, destruction; fifth, emptiness; and sixth, the great.
If these are further condensed, they become three *kalpas*: first, the small *kalpa* (which is the individual *kalpa*); second, the intermediate *kalpa* (either formation or abiding); and third...
Although the opening and closing of the great kalpa—comprising the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness—differ, they do not, in total, exceed the duration of a single great aeon.

Regarding the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*): it refers to the period following when the past world has already been destroyed and has remained empty for a long time, during which the karmic power of sentient beings [begins to manifest].
Furthermore, winds and rains arise once more to re-establish the various vessel-worlds (*bhājanaloka*). As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"The trichiliocosm is not accomplished by a single condition nor by a single event; it is accomplished through immeasurable conditions and immeasurable events.
That is to say, great clouds are spread abroad, a great rain is poured down, and the four kinds of winds [blow]."
What are the four [aspects] upon which the wheel’s continuity depends? First, it is capable of supporting, for it supports the great waters.
Second, it is capable of transforming, for it transforms the great waters. Third, it is called "establishment," for it establishes all locations.
Fourth, it is called "adornment," for its skillful distribution of adornments is excellent. All of these arise from the common karma of sentient beings and...
The roots of goodness from which all Bodhisattvas arise cause all sentient beings therein to receive and enjoy them, each according to their own suitability.
Furthermore, when the great clouds send down rain, there are great cloud-showers called "Able to Extinguish," which can extinguish the disaster of fire;
there are great cloud-showers called "Able to Arise," which can bring forth the great waters; and there are great cloud-showers called...
There is a great rain-cloud named "Able to Rest," which is able to rest the great waters; there is a great rain-cloud named "Able to Accomplish," which is able to accomplish all mani-jewels;
and there is a great rain-cloud named "Discrimination," which discriminates the trichiliocosm.
When the trichiliocosm was first being formed, the palaces of the gods of the Form Realm were formed first, followed by [the others].
The palaces of the various heavens of the desire realm are formed next, followed by the dwelling places for humans and other sentient beings.

Furthermore, it is like a great cloud raining down water of a single flavor, yet the palaces that arise differ in their variety according to the differences in the roots of goodness of the various sentient beings.
When the world is first about to be formed, there arises a great body of water that fills the trichiliocosm.

A great lotus flower arose in the world, named "The Jewel Adornment of the Merits of the Tathāgata’s Appearance," which covered the surface of the water and illuminated all worlds in the ten directions.

At that time, Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others, upon seeing this flower, knew with certainty that during this kalpa there would be that many Buddhas appearing in the world. Then, its...
Within this, there is a wind-circle named "Pure Radiance" (*śubhaprabhā*) that can form the palaces of the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*);
there is a wind-circle named "Adornment of Pure Radiance" (*vimalaprabhālaṃkāra*) that can form the palaces of the various devas of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*);
there is a wind-circle named "Solid and Impenetrable" (*dṛḍhasaṃhatābhedyā*) that can form the various Great and Small Cakravāḍa Mountains as well as the Vajra Mountains; and there is a wind...
There is a wind-circle named *Vivarta* (Turning) that is capable of forming Sumeru, the King of Mountains;
there is a wind-circle named *Acala* (Immovable) that is capable of forming the ten great mountain kings. What are these ten? They are:
Mount Khadiraka, Mount Ṛṣigiri, Mount Māraparājita, Mount Mahāmāraparājita, Mount Yugandhara, Mount Nimindhara, Mount Vinataka, Mount Aśvakarṇa, Mount Mahāmeru... [and so forth].
On Mount Cakravāḍa, Mount Gandhamādana, and Mount Himavat, there is a wind-circle named "Abiding" (*anuruddha*) which is able to form the great earth;
there is a wind-circle named "Adornment" (*vyūha*) which is able to form the palaces of the earth-dwelling devas, the palaces of the nāgas, and the palaces of the gandharvas;
and there is a wind-circle named "Inexhaustible Treasury" (*akṣaya-kośa*) which is able to form everything within the trichiliocosm.
In the great ocean, there is a wind-circle named Universal Radiance Treasury (*Samantaprabhā-kośa*) which can produce all the *maṇi* jewels of the trichiliocosm;
there is a wind-circle named Firm Root (*Dṛḍhamūla*) which can produce all the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*).
Although the water rained down by those great clouds is of a single flavor and without distinction, it becomes diverse according to the differences in the roots of goodness of sentient beings.
The wind-mandala differs; there are distinctions among wind-mandalas and distinctions among worlds.
The *Sūtra on the Arising of the World* (*Lokotpāda-sūtra*) states: "How does the world, having been destroyed, form again?

After the past world has been annihilated, after an immeasurable period of time has passed, great heavy clouds arise, covering the Brahma-heaven everywhere, and pour down a great torrential rain with drops as large as axle-trees, lasting for hundreds of thousands of millions of years."
That mass of rainwater gradually increases until it fills the great waters up to the Brahma-world, where it is sustained by the four winds.
After the rain ceases, the water recedes of its own accord for immeasurable billions of *yojanas*.
Then, a great wind named Anabhraka arises, blowing upon that mass of water so that the waves surge and boil, producing a vast mass of foam which it blows and places in the sky.
From the center, one constructs the palaces of the Brahmā heavens and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens (and so forth);

furthermore, one constructs Mount Sumeru, the Four Continents, the Cakravāḍa mountains, and so on, establishing them according to their ancient order (the creation of heaven and earth begins from this point).
When the world is formed, it first forms from above, beginning with the third dhyāna heaven of the Form Realm, and proceeds sequentially downward to the Yāma heaven of the Desire Realm.
This is because those who dwell in the sky [begin] from above and form [the world] downward;
next, starting from the wind-circle below, it is formed in successive order upward until reaching the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, as this depends upon the realm of earth, thus forming from below upward.
In this manner, through the stirring and transformation of wind and water over twenty kalpas, the receptacle world is finally accomplished.
The *sthāpya-kalpa* (abiding eon) refers to the period when the world has already been formed and enables sentient beings to dwell therein and enjoy its benefits.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Once the trichiliocosm has been fully accomplished, it brings benefit to immeasurable and diverse sentient beings."
That is to say, aquatic beings receive the benefit of water; terrestrial beings receive the benefit of land;
beings dwelling in palaces receive the benefit of palaces; and beings dwelling in space receive the benefit of space. The *Dīrgha Āgama* states:

"When heaven and earth were renewed, there was nothing at all, nor were there sun or moon. From the earth surged forth sweet springs (also called 'earth-flavor'), the taste of which was like [the finest honey]."
At the time of the appearance of clarified butter and honey, some gods from the Ābhāsvara Heaven whose merit was exhausted were reborn [at the beginning of human life].

Because they delighted in observing new lands and their natures were mostly fickle and restless, they tasted it with their fingers [the beginning of eating and drinking]. Thus, after three turns, they found its sweet flavor;

eating it incessantly, they gradually became coarse and fat, losing their celestial exquisite forms, supernormal powers, and radiance. Suddenly all became pitch black, and thereafter, great darkness prevailed.
A black wind blows upon the waters of the great ocean, casting forth the sun and moon (the beginning of day and night). They circle Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four continents;

when people see them emerge, they rejoice, and when they see them enter, they fear (the beginning of day and night). From this time onward, the cycles of day and night, the new and full moons, the seasons, and the years end and begin again.
At the time when the kalpa first formed, all beings were born by transformation, and there were no males or females.
Because they were born together in the world as a multitude of noble and base beings, they were called "sentient beings" (the origin of the name *sattva*).

Those who consumed much of the earth-flavor (*pṛthivī-rasa*) became coarse and haggard in appearance, while those who consumed little remained radiant and lustrous (the beginning of beauty and ugliness). Consequently, competition arose, leading to disputes between right and wrong (the beginning of unwholesome states).
As the earth-flavor gradually exhausted, everyone fell into distress, exclaiming, "Alas! What a calamity! There is no more earth-flavor! Then, earth-crust (*pṛthivī-parpaṭaka*) emerged.

The skin was like thin pancakes; when the surface of the earth vanished, it would reappear. Because the *pṛthivī-parpaṭaka* (earth-crust) vanished, it would again produce natural *medas* (earth-fat), which was like grape wine.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra) states: "When the earth-fat no longer grew, two-branched *drākṣā* (grapes)—that is, forest creepers—arose.
Their flavor was also sweet. After eating them for a long time in great quantities, they began to mock one another, saying, 'Grapes!'"
The rice grew spontaneously and was free of husks and chaff; though it required no seasoning, it possessed all manner of exquisite flavors.
When sentient beings ate it, they produced male and female forms (the beginning of having roots). The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:

"The naturally grown, non-seeded fragrant rice was coarse as food, and thus waste remained within the body. To eliminate this, two passages [the urinary and reproductive tracts] subsequently arose, resulting in males and females."
The arising of the sense organs occurs because of their form; thus, the habituation of desire begins. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"At that time, those among people who possessed much desire became women, hence the name 'husband and wife' (the beginning of matrimony). Subsequently, as the lustful desires of sentient beings increased further, they began to dwell together as couples.
Later, beings descended from the Ābhāsvara Heaven into the womb, (the beginning of viviparity); hence there is the womb."
At that time of birth, cities and walls were established, and wild rice grew spontaneously: if harvested in the morning, it ripened by evening; if harvested in the evening, it ripened by morning.
According to the *Madhyama Āgama*, when the rice was four inches long and had not yet developed stalks or stems, sentient beings began taking up their daily ration all at once;
others followed this example until they took up five days' worth of wild rice at once. Consequently, the rice gradually developed husks and chaff, and once harvested, it no longer grew back.
Thereupon, there was a withered stump. At that time, the sentient beings were distressed and wept bitterly;

they each demarcated their fields and houses with non-glutinous rice as boundary markers (the beginning of cultivated fields). Among them, some would hide their own rice and steal grain from the fields of others, yet no one could adjudicate such matters.
They deliberated on establishing a single impartial lord to protect the people well, rewarding the virtuous and punishing the wicked, and each agreed to reduce their own shares to provide for him.
Therefore, one person of noble appearance and great talent and virtue was selected and requested to serve as lord (the beginning of the lordship over the fields, like the present kings).
Thus, for the first time, there arose the name "Lord of the People" (*minzhǔ*). He practiced the ten wholesome deeds and took pity on the people as parents love their children;
the people revered the lord as children revere their father. Human life was long, and abundance and joy were limitless. — *Āgama*.
When the world was first formed, the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended; each possessed a natural radiance and traveled with sovereign ease.

Seeing the "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka), which was exceedingly fragrant and delicious, those who consumed it in excess immediately lost their supernormal powers of flight, became heavy-bodied, and their radiance vanished.

Thereupon, the sun and moon first appeared. Because of their greed for food, the earth-fat perished. After the earth-fat had vanished, the *bāluka* (gravel) appeared; after the *bāluka* had vanished, [the forest grew].
The raw non-glutinous rice grows to about four inches in length; it is harvested in the morning and regrows by evening.

Because they eat that rice, the male and female characteristics become distinct, and they engage in unchaste conduct. They then establish households, and among them, sentient beings who are indolent think to themselves:
"Let us take a large amount of non-glutinous rice for one day's food," and so on, until they accumulate enough for seven days. As the rice is harvested, it regrows by evening.

They no longer gave rise [to such thoughts]. (Master Yu said: "Once the corrupt winds have stirred, the pure source is exhausted; when spirits and essences communicate through resonance, a thunderbolt strikes with delayed force. When taxes were increased in Donglai, the sea fish retreated to swim in hiding; when levies were raised at Hepu, the pearl oysters moved far away.
Comparing the present with the past, it is not surprising that non-glutinous rice did not grow there. Because of this, the cultivation of fields was established as a formal institution.
Then, a certain sentient being entered another's field and stole another's rice, whereupon they began to fight and box with one another. The sentient beings all raised [the alarm].
First, the wise take *samādhi* as the guardian of their fields; if there is anyone who should reprimand them, they shall cause that person to reprimand them.
Whatever rice we obtain, we shall deliver it to this guardian of the fields—this is called the Kṣatriya caste.

Those who leave home to enter the mountains in search of the Way, distancing themselves from unwholesome dharmas, are called the Brāhmaṇa caste. Those who practice their occupations to provide for themselves are called the Vaiśya.
Those of the kṣatriya caste who practice various arts and crafts as their livelihood are called śūdras (or vaiśyas).
Among these four castes, there are those who reflect that worldly affection is defiled and impure; what is there to crave?
Therefore, they leave home, shave their hair and beards, and seek the Way in dharma robes. Such are the śramaṇas. (The commentator says: The title "śramaṇa" has existed since ancient times.)

Desire is the root of suffering and the source of attachment; because this attachment is deep, all evils arise together. Because desire flourishes, birth and death are endless. Therefore, the bodhisattvas of antiquity, through self-awakening, realized their error and immediately renounced affection to block the source of suffering.

They further abandoned the attachment to home to sever the cause of evil. This is like a bird escaping from its cage or the moon emerging from the clouds—the path that transcends the mundane dust truly begins with this.

Within this abiding kalpa (*sthāpya-kalpa*), heaven and earth do not perish and sentient beings dwell in peace for another twenty minor kalpas (*antara-kalpa*). During each minor kalpa, when the period of increase reaches its peak:
When a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world during the period of extreme decline, there occurs a minor triad of calamities (detailed below).

Regarding the "kalpa of destruction" (*saṃvarta-kalpa*): this refers to the complete destruction and extinction of all things in the world once the kalpa of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*) has reached its full term. *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
It is said that when the kalpa-fire arises in the trichiliocosm, it incinerates all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests,
as well as the Cakravāḍa and Mahācakravāḍa mountains, until everything is consumed by flames without remainder. Furthermore, when the calamity of wind arises,
there is a great wind called "Dissolution" (*saṃvartanī*) capable of destroying the Cakravāḍa mountains and other features of the trichiliocosm.
All are reduced to fine dust. Furthermore, there is a great wind called "The Obstructing," which encircles the trichiliocosm;

it obstructs and scatters the winds of destruction so that they do not reach other world-systems. If this great obstructing wind did not exist, there would be no world-system in the ten directions that would not be utterly destroyed.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Xianzong lun) states: "As for the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), it refers to the hells..."

There are two ways in which sentient beings no longer arise until the destruction of the external receptacle world: first, the destruction of the destinies (*gati*), and second, the destruction of the realms (*dhātu*).
Regarding the destruction of the destinies: after twenty intermediate kalpas have passed in this world, there follows another twenty intermediate kalpas of the "subsistence" period;
at the point when the kalpa of destruction is about to begin, the lifespan of humans dwelling on this continent is eighty thousand years, and at that time, the hells [are empty].
When sentient beings pass away and no new ones are born, this marks the beginning of the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*). This continues until not a single sentient being remains in the hells;

at that time, it is said that the hells have been destroyed. Regarding those with karma fixed for the various hells, the force of their karma draws them and places them in the hells of other directions.
By this analogy, one should understand that when the realms of animals (*tiryagyoni*) and hungry ghosts (*preta*) are likewise destroyed, there are no [such beings] within the bodies of humans.
Because the insects and the Buddha’s body are both animals, there are two explanations regarding their destruction: those that benefit humans perish along with them, while others perish first.
At that time, a single person on this continent of the human realm spontaneously attains the first dhyāna without a teacher and proclaims these words:
"The joy and bliss born of seclusion are most excellent and most tranquil. Having heard this, all other people likewise enter into meditative concentration.
At the end of their lives, they are all reborn in the Brahma-world; when sentient beings in this continent have been completely exhausted, this is called the destruction of the people of Jambudvīpa.

By analogy with this, when the inhabitants of the eastern and western continents perish, they are likewise [reborn]. As for those in the northern continent, at the end of their lives, they are reborn in the heavens of the desire realm because, having dull faculties, they lack the capacity for detachment from desire.
Having been born in the desire heavens, they must manifest dhyāna and subsequently attain a superior basis before they can achieve detachment from desire.

When not even a single sentient being remains in the human realm such that the human realm can be said to have been destroyed, at that time, a certain sentient being in the desire realm—spontaneously and without a teacher—attains the first dhyāna and is reborn in the Brahma world. This continues until not even a single sentient being remains in the desire realm such that the desire realm can be said to have been destroyed.
At that time, a certain sentient being in the Brahma world—spontaneously and without a teacher—[attains the second dhyāna].
Upon attaining the second dhyāna, they utter these words: "The joy and bliss born of concentration are most pleasant and most tranquil.

When the other devas hear this, they all enter that dhyāna; at the end of their lives, they are reborn together in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, until finally all sentient beings up to the Brahma-world have been exhausted.
(It should be understood that this applies similarly upward to the destruction of the third dhyāna. Only the vessel world remains empty and vast until the great calamity is about to arise.
The destruction of the realms (*dhātu-vināśa*). "Destruction of the realms" refers to the destruction of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) by the calamities of fire, water, and wind.

1. The Fire Kalpa: A fire arises simultaneously with it, destroying [the world] up to the Second Dhyāna Heaven. 2. The Water Kalpa: Water arises simultaneously with it, destroying [the world] up to the Third Dhyāna Heaven. 3. The Wind Kalpa:
Wind arises simultaneously with it, destroying [the world] up to the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven; however, the Fourth Dhyāna Heaven is not [destroyed].

Because it is destroyed for the sake of purifying equanimity and mindfulness, this great kalpa of the three calamities destroys only the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) and does not destroy sentient beings (*sattva*).
Sentient beings either migrate to other realms or, if they possess the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), vows, or *samādhi*, they attain rebirth within the heavens of the fourth dhyāna.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "The heavens of the three lower dhyānas will inevitably encounter the calamities of water, fire, and wind."
In the first dhyāna, vitarka and vicāra are the internal calamities that burn and afflict the mind, corresponding to the external fire disaster;
in the second dhyāna, the feeling of joy (*prīti*) is the internal calamity, corresponding to the external water disaster due to its moistening nature;

in the third dhyāna, the movement of breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) is the internal calamity, corresponding to the external wind disaster. Thus, the first dhyāna possesses three internal calamities and likewise encounters three external disasters.
The second dhyāna is destroyed by two internal calamities and likewise by two external calamities;

the third dhyāna is destroyed by one internal calamity and likewise by one external calamity; the fourth dhyāna has no external calamities because within that meditative state there are no internal afflictions.
*Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*: Question: Why does the kalpa of destruction not reach the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: Because they are born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), which are the unsurpassed stages, they attain parinirvāṇa right there;
furthermore, they do not descend to lower stages, as such descent is not subject to cessation through non-cultivation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Nor is it the case that they remain there even through the destruction of an eon (*kalpa-saṃvarta*), for they are born in those places by the power of their superior merit. If internal disturbance were to occur within those stages, then external [disturbance] would follow.
Regarding calamities: because the first dhyāna is internally disturbed by the fire of vitarka and vicāra, it is externally consumed by the calamity of fire;
because the second dhyāna is internally disturbed by the water of joy (prīti), it is externally swept away by the calamity of water;

because the third dhyāna is internally disturbed by the wind of inhalation and exhalation (āśvāsa-praśvāsa), it is externally destroyed by the calamity of wind. One might ask: does the fourth dhyāna not likewise possess such disturbances?

Question: Why is it that the disordered [state] is not permanent? Answer: Because it is destroyed by momentary impermanence. In the stage of the fourth dhyāna, the signs are not fixed in their continuity;
they arise together with the palaces of the deities born there, and when those deities' lives end, they likewise perish along with them.
Whenever the kalpa of abiding ends, it must necessarily pass through one fire calamity that destroys the world-system; this destruction is completed only after twenty small kalpas have elapsed.
The kalpas of water and wind destruction shall be explained as follows.

Regarding the "empty kalpa" (śūnya-kalpa): this refers to the period following a great catastrophe when the heavens, the earth, and all things have entirely lost their forms, leaving only a vast, empty void.
Such an emptiness likewise endures for twenty minor kalpas; once these kalpas have passed, it enters the kalpa of formation again.
As in the preceding kalpa, the winds of the kalpa blow and stir up the waters of the kalpa, producing thick foam that transforms into the mountains and seas of the future world,
which is established just as before.
This is the diagram of the great kalpa’s cycle of formation and destruction.
Taken together, these four types constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). This great kalpa undergoes a cycle of formation and destruction that continues incessantly.
All worlds throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time possess these four phases of the kalpa:

formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. Once formed, they abide; while abiding, they continue toward destruction; having been destroyed, they become empty again; and from emptiness, they form once more. This process repeats in succession.

The Cycle is Endless (For example, it takes twenty years to construct a floating bridge; another twenty years for people to cross over it; another twenty years for it to gradually decay until it is gone; and another twenty years when there is no bridge, only water. This water represents the empty kalpa. Furthermore, one great kalpa is like one great year:

the four intermediate kalpas are like the four seasons—formation is like spring, abiding is like summer, destruction is like autumn, and emptiness is like winter; and from winter, it returns again to spring).

The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "In this way, in the eastern direction, there are immeasurable worlds, uninterrupted and without interval, some of which are about to be destroyed, some about to be formed, some currently being destroyed, some already destroyed and empty, some currently being formed, and some already formed and abiding.
As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in all ten directions. Thus it is for both the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) and the physical world (*bhājanaloka*)."
Because they are produced by the power of intervening karma and afflictions, and because they arise through the predominance of karma and afflictions.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "For example, in a forest, leaves are both born and fall; likewise, within these world-systems, worlds undergo formation and destruction.
The *Zhuangchun Lu* says: "Observing that the formation and destruction of worlds are infinite, there are two causes and conditions: first, due to the multitude [of beings]..."
First, that which is induced by the karma of shared birth: this refers to being moved by the deluded karma of the three poisons within the single mind.
Since the deluded karma has not yet been exhausted, how could the dependent retribution ever end? If there were no basis for it, what would be called "receiving retribution"?

Therefore, the formation and destruction of worlds proceed in continuous succession. Second, that which is induced by the power of the Buddhas' vows: this refers to the Buddhas possessing great vows to exhaustively deliver all sentient beings. The multitude... [text truncated]
Since birth is inexhaustible, the Buddha’s vows are likewise endless; thus, the resultant dependent retribution continues in succession.
Regarding the diagram of the cycles of increase and decrease within the minor kalpas:

within one great kalpa, there is one kalpa of formation and one kalpa of abiding, each containing twenty minor kalpas. Within these minor kalpas— [text truncated] —the cycles of increase and decrease proceed in rotation.
This refers to one period of increase and one period of decrease; these increases and decreases are explained in terms of human lifespan.

The kalpa of decrease proceeds from the upper right, gradually diminishing downward until the lifespan reaches ten years. These figures for the increase and decrease of lifespan are based on the *Madhyama Āgama*.

The *utkalpa* (increasing eon) gradually increases from the bottom left up to eighty thousand [years]. White is used as a metaphor for the wholesome (*śubha*), and black as a metaphor for the unwholesome (*aśubha*).
The commentary states: The sūtras refer to these as *utkarṣāpakarṣakalpa* (increasing and decreasing eons), explaining their meaning primarily through the wholesome.
That is to say, "increase" refers to the growth of virtuous karma, whereby merit increases, lifespan increases, and so forth, up to...
When the ten wholesome actions are fully realized, the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, which is the maximum limit of the increasing eon (*vivartakalpa*).
Just as the moon gradually increases its brightness from the first and second days until the fifteenth day when the lunar light is perfectly full, so too does the black fortnight reach its end;
the decrease occurs because wholesome karma is diminished.
Because of this decrease, merit decreases, lifespan decreases, and so forth, until the ten wholesome deeds are exhausted;
at that time, when the human lifespan is ten years, it constitutes the limit of the *kṣaya-kalpa* (the aeon of decrease).
Just as on the sixteenth or seventeenth day of the moon the light gradually diminishes until, on the thirtieth night, the bright phase of the moon has vanished and only the dark remains.
The Moon establishes the names "increase" and "decrease" based on the increase of virtue and the decrease of virtue in this world.
When the lifespan increases to eighty thousand years, the seven treasures appear, the five flavors become sweet and delicious, and all hundredfold blessings gather together.

Humans and spirits are harmonious and joyful; wind and rain come at their proper times; fragrant rice and sweet springs abound; the world is filled with virtuous people, and a Wheel-Turning King appears. Abundant...
When bliss reaches its limit and human lifespans diminish to ten years, the seven treasures vanish; the five flavors become bitter and astringent; a hundred misfortunes converge;
humanity is reduced to extremity and things to suffering; ghosts wail and spirits cry out; yin and yang are in discord;

wind and rain lose their proper seasons; famine and pestilence prevail; people slaughter one another with cruelty; they are foolish, depraved, and evil, possessing barely a human form—such is the ultimate limit of decay.

It is said that the accumulation of good brings down blessings, while the accumulation of evil brings down calamities; how could one not believe this? Having previously clarified the increase and decrease [of karma], we shall now explain them alternately.
This means that when good increases, evil decreases; when good decreases, evil increases.

If there is one part of good, there are nine parts of evil; if there are two parts of good, there are eight parts of evil; continuing thus until there are nine parts of good, there is one part of evil; and when there are ten parts of good, there is no evil at all.

This is what is meant by the "extreme of increase" (which is also the extreme of the decrease of evil). For instance, when evil is one part, good is nine parts; when evil is two parts, good is eight parts; continuing until evil is nine parts, good is one part;
and when evil reaches ten parts, there is no good at all. This is what is meant by the "extreme of decrease" (which is also the extreme of the increase of evil).
It is just as when yang grows, yin diminishes, and when yin grows, yang diminishes; for it is precisely because the good and evil within the human heart mutually diminish one another.

Because of this increase, the conditions for retribution—suffering and pleasure—undergo fluctuations, manifesting as signs of augmentation and diminution. Thus we know that cause and effect are distinct and clear, and their resonance is without error.
