One complete cycle of such increase and decrease is called a *kṣudra-kalpa* (small kalpa). Twenty cycles revolving in this manner constitute one *mahā-kalpa* (great kalpa) of abiding.
Someone may ask: "How do these images of increase and decrease, the lifespans, and their meanings correspond to the hexagrams of the *Yi*?"

The Qi is entirely identical to the *Yī* (Book of Changes), wherein Yin and Yang alternately undergo waxing and waning. When Yang reaches its ultimate limit, Yin arises; when Yin reaches its ultimate limit, Yang arises.
This cycle proceeds without end, for such is the inevitable force of the dynamics of Qi and number (*shù*).

If this is so, and good and evil likewise alternate in their waxing and waning, then it follows that when goodness reaches its ultimate limit, evil must arise, and when evil reaches its ultimate limit, goodness must arise. Would it then be possible for the wicked to become good?

"Is it that evil acts as the cause for one another, or that perversity acts as the cause for one another? This would constitute a perverse cause. If the cause is perverse, then both cause and effect are not what they should be;
yet the sequence of cause and effect remains distinct—where, then, is the fruit? The answer is: "It is not that good arises from evil, nor is it that evil arises from good.
When people at the end of a kalpa suffer to the extreme, they long for happiness; when things reach their limit, they know how to turn back. Thus, the innate goodness of the heart [is restored]."

Because one currently reforms evil into goodness, sins are extinguished and blessings arise; this is a case of turning away from evil to become good, not that goodness arises from the ultimate limit of evil.
If one does not turn back when evil has reached its extreme, one will flow into hell—how could there be any principle by which blessings and longevity increase?

Furthermore, at a time of flourishing prosperity, while dwelling in a state where blessings are full, one becomes arrogant, extravagant, and unrestrained, abandoning goodness and indulging in evil; thus, evil is discharged and sin is incurred.
To come [from good] is to lose the good and become evil; it is not that the ultimate limit of good gives rise to evil.

If one does not grow weary of the ultimate limit of good, one abandons the human realm and is reborn in a celestial palace. How could there be any principle of premature death or the exhaustion of blessings?

One may only say that good serves as a cause for increase and evil serves as a cause for decrease; one must not say that good is the cause of evil or that evil is the cause of good. Therefore, there is increase and decrease.
The mutual interaction of these phenomena and the waxing and waning of yin and yang are fundamentally identical; their increase and decrease arise from the mind, not from numerical calculation.
Therefore, those who hold views based on causes or no-cause are inferior and ignorant, being confined by quantitative measures.
Superior sages transcend quantitative measures and are not turned by external objects. This [section] summarizes the general characteristics of the present kalpa to provide an explanation.

The meaning of their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) is fully detailed in the various sūtras and śāstras. Regarding the method of the increase and decrease of the minor kalpas (*antara-kalpa*), according to the *Zhuangchun ji* (Collection on Zhuangzi and Chongyu):
at the beginning of this abiding kalpa (*sthiti-kalpa*), the lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa was eighty-four thousand years and their height was eight zhang.

For every hundred years that pass, the lifespan decreases by one year and the body height decreases by one cun; for every thousand years, the lifespan decreases by ten years and the body [height]... [decreases].
It decreases by one foot; thus it continues to decrease until at the age of ten, the height of the body is one foot, which marks the limit of the kalpa of decrease.
After this, the world enters the kalpa of increase. For every hundred years that pass, the lifespan increases by one year and the height of the body increases by one inch.
This continues to increase until the lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years.

When the human body increases by eight *zhang*, it marks the limit of an increase in the *kalpa*. Thus, one decrease and one increase together total 1,680,000 years, which is called one *vartanī-kalpa* (a "wheel-turning" kalpa).
Only after twenty such *vartanī-kalpas* does one complete *sthiti-kalpa* (a "residing" kalpa) occur. [Commentary:
Generally speaking, the discourse on increase and decrease is for the time being as described above. However, if we examine this in detail once more, it is not so.
However, according to the total sum of the *zhāng* and *chūn*, this is correct; yet the claim that his body was eight *zhàng* tall represents the ultimate limit of increase is incorrect.
Why? Because when a human body is eight *zhàng* tall, the lifespan is only eight hundred years. How could it decrease immediately after reaching the peak of eight hundred years?
Furthermore, how could there ever be a Wheel-Turning King appearing in the world with such a lifespan? If this were the case, then increase and decrease would merely...
One hundred and sixty-eight thousand years constitutes but one-hundredth part of the aforementioned total.
Although it is said that [the lifespan] increases to eighty-four thousand years, this refers to the number of years elapsed, not the actual human lifespan.
If one were to claim that the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, then the height of such a person would necessarily be eight hundred and forty *zhang*.
The years that have passed amount to eight million four hundred thousand; this is precisely the maximum number for the period of increase, and the decrease follows the same pattern.
Furthermore, it is said that when the lifespan reaches ten years and the height is one chi, this constitutes the limit of decrease.

However, if one were to claim that the decrease continues beyond eighty-four thousand years until the body has shrunk by eight zhang to constitute the limit of decrease, that would also be incorrect. Why is this so? Suppose the decrease...
During the eighty-four thousand years [that have passed], the human body has decreased by eight *zhang*; at this time, the human lifespan is now decreasing toward eight hundred years.

There remain eighty-three thousand one hundred and some years of life, and the height of the body remains at eight hundred thirty-one *zhang* and more (at this stage, the lifespan is certainly not ten years, nor is the body one foot tall).
How could this be considered the ultimate limit of decrease? This shall be further clarified by means of a diagram.
During the kalpa of increase (beginning from a human lifespan of ten years):
as the lifespan increases by one year every hundred years, the body height increases by one cun.
After one thousand years, the lifespan increases by ten years and the stature increases by one chi;
after ten thousand years, the lifespan increases by one hundred years and the stature increases by one zhang;
after one hundred thousand years, the lifespan increases by one thousand years and the stature increases by ten zhang.
Exceeding one million [years], increasing by ten thousand years; increasing by one hundred *zhang*;
exceeding eight million [years], increasing by eighty thousand years; increasing by eight hundred *zhang*;
(further exceeding four hundred thousand years); (further adding four thousand years); (further adding forty *zhang*).
During the aeon of decrease (beginning from a human lifespan of eighty-four thousand years):
with each passing century, the lifespan decreases by one year and the body height decreases by one inch.
After a thousand years, [the lifespan] decreases by ten years and [the stature] decreases by one chi;
after ten thousand years, it decreases by one hundred years and [the stature] decreases by one zhang;
after one hundred thousand years, it decreases by one thousand years and [the stature] decreases by ten zhang.
When [the lifespan] exceeds one million [years], the height decreases by ten thousand *zhang*;
when it exceeds eight million [years], the height decreases by eighty thousand *zhang*.

(Furthermore, after thirty-nine thousand nine hundred years have passed,) [the lifespan] decreases by three thousand nine hundred and ninety years, and the height decreases by three thousand nine hundred and ninety *zhang*, until only one *zhang* remains.
If it is said that "every hundred years, one year is added," it should be understood according to this diagram;
otherwise, it would not mean that one year is added every hundred years (to be further examined).
Regarding the four wheel-turning kings during the aeon of increase:
throughout every aeon of increase, there are four types of wheel-turning kings who appear in succession in the world, as previously described.

When the human lifespan gradually increases to twenty thousand years, an iron-wheel-turning king appears in the world; he rules over one continent, establishing order through the exertion of his majesty. Furthermore, [the lifespan] continues to increase.
When the lifespan of humans reaches forty thousand years, a copper-wheel-turning king appears in the world; he rules over two continents, and his majesty is so formidable that they submit.
When the lifespan increases to sixty thousand years, a silver-wheel-turning king appears in the world; he rules over three continents, and they submit only after he dispatches envoys.
When the lifespan increases to eighty thousand years, a gold-wheel-turning king appears in the world; he rules over the four continents, and all look upon him with awe and majesty.
The Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel in Śrāvastī possessed the seven treasures and a thousand sons; he transformed the world through the ten wholesome deeds. As for the seven treasures:
first is the golden wheel treasure, made of pure gold and complete with a thousand spokes, which arrived flying through the air on the day of the king’s consecration.
By the power of this wheel, the king and his fourfold army traveled through the air, circling the four continents; all the minor kings looked up to him in reverence.
1. The Elephant Treasure: Two elephants that have been converted [to his service], white as the Snow Mountains and endowed with six tusks.

2. The Horse Treasure: Born of the Dragon lineage, which the King mounts to travel around the four continents in a single day. 3. The Woman Treasure: Born from a lotus, of supreme beauty and the foremost in excellence.
4. The Military Commander Treasure: Brave, powerful, and possessing matchless wisdom and strategy. 5. The Treasurer Treasure: Skilled in the knowledge of [hidden] treasures.

The hidden treasures were at the king’s disposal for his use; the seven *cintāmaṇi* jewels radiated light for one *yojana*, making the night like day, and furthermore, according to the king’s wish, they rained down various precious gems.
The king lived for eighty-four thousand years, and the succession was passed to his eldest son.

At that time, the seven treasures (gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and so forth) appeared, and the essence of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) rose up from the ground, naturally producing non-glutinous rice throughout the four seasons.
Those of gentle conduct who practice the ten wholesome paths attain the utmost abundance and joy for a vast duration of time (as detailed in various sūtras and śāstras).
Regarding the minor three calamities at the end of a kalpa of decrease:
at the conclusion of every kalpa of decrease, these minor three calamities arise in succession. According to the Abhidharma-śāstra, the Buddha said:

Within a kalpa, the world undergoes twenty intermediate kalpas of destruction, followed by twenty intermediate kalpas of emptiness after destruction, followed by twenty intermediate kalpas of formation after emptiness, and finally twenty intermediate kalpas of abiding after formation.
During this period of abiding, three minor calamities revolve in succession: first, the calamity of pestilence; second, the calamity of weapons.
Regarding the first minor calamity of the three calamities of famine: when this first minor calamity arises, there will be a great epidemic of various diseases.

The lifespan of the people of Jambudvīpa will be shortened until it is only ten years; their bodies will be stunted, measuring only two or three spans (vitasti) in height. Coarse millet will be considered the finest food, and wearing hair-cloth will be the primary mode of dress.
These people will not practice the True Dharma, and false views will increase. Malevolent spirits will harm the people, and kings will all perish, leaving the lands desolate.

The lands lie desolate, with only small prefectures and counties remaining, separated by vast distances; there is no remedy for the suffering of illness, and in a single day and night, immeasurable numbers die from pestilence.
Because they practiced evil dharmas, they receive this retribution, being born into this age of turbidity (*kalpa-kaṣāya*).

The prefectures and counties become overgrown and ruined, with only a few households remaining, their locations becoming increasingly remote. With no one to provide burial, white bones cover the ground. At the end of the kalpa, during the seven days of the masses...

When the epidemic had caused everyone to die except for ten thousand people who were able to maintain virtuous conduct and were protected by benevolent deities so that the lineage was not severed, after seven days the great plague subsided and the malevolent spirits dispersed.
Thereupon, the yin and yang were harmonized and delicious flavors emerged;
sentient beings beheld one another as if they were close kin, loving one another with joy, and they did not abandon the wholesome Dharma, but increased in it.

(Virtue-increase is the cause for the increase of the aeon. As the lifespan gradually increases to twenty thousand years, and after a long time increases further to eighty thousand years, women marry at the age of five hundred.
The lands are prosperous and joyful, villages are situated close together, and clothing, wealth, and treasures are fully provided according to one's wishes.
This continues for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* years (this is the period when the increase reaches its peak), until sentient beings have not yet given rise to the ten [unwholesome paths of action].

From the arising of evil, the ten non-virtuous actions increase (the commission of evil acts serves as the cause for decline). Lifespans gradually diminish until they reach ten years (the ultimate limit of this decline). Regarding the calamity of weapons:
when the human lifespan is ten years, the three poisons and false views increase day and night; fathers, sons, and brothers fight and quarrel with one another, let alone others;
they terrify each other with tiles, stones, swords, and staves, and the various kingdoms of the four directions [engage in mutual conflict].
Mutually attacking and slaying one another, they will die in immeasurable numbers; as a result of these unwholesome karmic fruits, they will be born in this *kalpa*-turbidity.

When families are utterly destroyed and only the remnants remain scattered, at the end of the *kalpa*, for seven days, people will take grass and wood in their hands, which will instantly become swords and staves, with which they will slaughter one another.
At that time, terrified of these weapons, some people will flee into mountain forests, onto solitary islands, or into pits and caves to avoid the calamities; or—
At that time, upon seeing one another, they would still flee in terror, like deer encountering a hunter. For seven days, immeasurable beings met their deaths by the sword;
only ten thousand remained to serve as the seed of humanity (as described previously). After the seven days had passed, the violence ceased and the yin and yang were harmonized.
When sentient beings saw one another, they felt affection as if toward close kin. From the age of ten, they gradually practiced virtue.
The lifespan increases from twenty thousand up to eighty thousand years, remaining for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* aeons (as before).
During the period of famine, the human lifespan is ten years; people eat weeds and barnyard grass, wear human hair as clothing, and endure poverty and suffering.
Ignorance and false views increase day and night. Grain becomes so precious that famine prevails; seeing the provisions of others, they go to seize their food. By this cause...
Because of the immeasurable evil karma created by starving to death, there was no rain for four or five years;

due to this great drought, even wild grasses and vegetables could not be found, let alone rice or grain. Countless people died of hunger day and night, and the districts and counties were emptied, with only a few households remaining.
At that time, when the three poisons increased further, there was no rain for six or seven years of great drought, and [the people] longed [for relief].
Even water cannot be found when one looks for it, let alone food and drink;

at the end of the kalpa, after seven days, those who die of hunger are nearly exhausted, with only ten thousand people remaining (as previously described), until life expectancy increases again to eighty thousand years. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that three kinds of minor calamities appear, namely:
famine, disease, and the sword. As for the calamity of famine, it first begins to manifest when the human lifespan is thirty years.
At that time, exquisite food and drink can no longer be obtained; people can only hold banquets together using boiled, withered bones.
If they encounter even a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or barnyard grass, they regard it as precious as a mani jewel, placing it in a chest or basket to guard it.
Due to this famine, the classes of sentient beings perish almost entirely. This calamity of scarcity lasts for seven years.
Only on the seventh day of the seventh month do those sentient beings attain passage [to a higher realm];

through this cause and condition, their lifespan ceases to diminish and the calamity of famine is finally stilled. When the human lifespan reaches twenty years, they abandon the aversion they previously felt.
At that time, pestilential vapors arise in succession, and all those sentient beings [fall ill].
Many perish in this manner; after seven months and seven days have passed, this calamity of disease finally subsides. Those sentient beings then give rise to a moderate sense of weary detachment.
By virtue of this cause and condition, their lifespan does not decrease further, and the calamity of disease ceases.
When human life expectancy reaches ten years, those who previously felt weary and afflicted now again abandon that feeling. At that time, when sentient beings see one another, each...
Giving rise to a mind of fierce violence, by reason of this, even the grasses, trees, tiles, and stones they grasp become swords and blades with which they slaughter one another;
only after seven days have passed do they finally emerge from it. Furthermore, there are three kinds of extreme decline:
first, the decline of lifespan, meaning that the maximum lifespan reaches only ten years; second, the decline of the physical basis, meaning...
Their physical stature reaches a maximum of only one span or a single fist; their three requisites are in decline, and they subsist solely on millet and wild panicled millet as food.
Among these, the first [type] wears garments of hair, the second wears iron as their ornament, and the third likewise.
All five kinds of superior flavors have completely vanished—namely, ghee, honey, sugarcane, oil, and salt—and all tastes have been transformed.
At that time, sentient beings gathered together and gave rise to a supreme sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*), which never again declined;
they were further able to abandon those unwholesome and evil dharmas that diminish lifespan, and practiced and cultivated those wholesome dharmas that increase lifespan.
By these causes and conditions, their lifespan, physical strength, wealth, happiness, and sovereignty all gradually increased until it reached eighty thousand years. (From the Madhyama Āgama)

The Sūtra states: When the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, people first began to commit the evil of stealing the property of others. Because such theft proliferated, their longevity and physical stature gradually diminished;

while the father’s lifespan was eighty thousand years, the son’s lifespan was only forty thousand. At that time, because sentient beings increased their karmic actions of killing, their lifespan decreased by twenty thousand years.

Furthermore, because they increased false speech and double-tongued slander, their lifespan decreased by ten thousand years. Subsequently, as jealousy and sexual misconduct further increased, [the lifespan continued to decline].
...down to the point where, due to unrighteous desires, evil and perverse greed, double-tongued speech, frivolous talk, wrong views, lack of filial piety toward parents, disrespect for śramaṇas,

failure to perform meritorious deeds, and a failure to perceive the retribution of future lives, the lifespan decreases further by five thousand, two thousand, one thousand, fifteen hundred, two hundred,
one hundred years, until finally, when the human lifespan is ten years, a girl is born at only five months of age.
When the *priyaṅgu* grain is harvested, its flavor is sweet and exquisite; it vanishes entirely except for those who practice the ten unwholesome deeds, who are nevertheless revered by others.

The people harbor mutual intent to harm one another (the arising of the *śastra-kalpa* is the same as in the Abhidharma). Yet there are also those possessed of shame and remorse who feel weary of and loathe [this state], so they enter the mountains and wilds to hide away.
After the *śastra-kalpa* has passed, they emerge from the mountains and wilds; seeing one another again, they possess mutual hearts of compassion and affection.
It was as if kinsmen had said: "Because we gave rise to unwholesome thoughts, we have caused our kin to die out completely.

We would rather practice wholesome dharmas together and abstain from the act of killing. Having practiced wholesome deeds, their lifespan increased by ten years, and they bore sons whose lifespan was twenty years.
They then thought: "If one practices wholesome deeds, both lifespan and physical appearance improve; we should [continue to do so]."
They further increased their practice of virtue by abandoning taking what is not given, whereby their lifespan increased by forty years. Furthermore, by abandoning sexual misconduct,

false speech, up to divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, as well as greed, envy, malice, wrong views, unrighteous desires, evil and perverse greed, and the practice of unwholesome dharmas,
their lifespan increased by eighty, one hundred and sixty-three, three hundred and sixty, two thousand, five hundred, and six thousand [years] respectively.

When human life spans reach ten thousand, twenty thousand, forty thousand, or eighty thousand years, people will be filial toward their parents, respectful toward śramaṇas, and cultivate various meritorious deeds.

This Jambudvīpa will be exceedingly prosperous and joyful; women shall not marry until they are five hundred years old, and the wheel-turning monarchs (cakravartin) will rule the world while the people live in peace and happiness (*etc.*).
Regarding pestilence and famine, the extension or contraction [of their duration] is the same as previously stated. *Xinpo* (New Commentary).

The *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* states: "If there is one who can observe the precept against killing for a single day and night, they will certainly not encounter the outbreak of the calamity of weapons in future lives.

If one can offer even a single *harītakī* fruit with a mind of profound purity to the Saṃgha, they will certainly not encounter the calamity of disease in future lives. If one can offer even a single morsel of food..."
All sentient beings will certainly not encounter the calamity of famine in future ages. [Commentary:

Observing the increase and decrease of kalpas, the extension and contraction of human lifespans, the abundance and scarcity of lands, and the suffering or joy of enjoyments—all these depend upon karma.
The good or evil of karma is governed by the human mind; as the human mind becomes pure or frivolous, they mutually encroach upon one another.
Because good and evil nourish one another, the increase or decrease of kalpas and the prolongation or shortening of lifespans follow suit.
Truly, the retribution for good and evil follows like a shadow follows its form; the signs of suffering and joy have always been interchanged in this way.

Therefore, we who now possess the most supreme intelligence ought to cease the ten unwholesome deeds and diligently practice the ten wholesome deeds, so that the fruit may manifest in every successive life.
Those who receive auspicious rewards and sublime blessings—will they not surely enjoy a state of carefree serenity with abundant leisure?

Regarding the signs of the three great calamities, all the physical world-systems (*bhājana-loka*), having existed for a long time, must inevitably perish; there are three kinds of great calamities that arise in due course, the first being fire.

Regarding "calamities" (*upadrava*): this refers to how, at the end of a *mahākalpa*, once the period of abiding (*sthiti-kalpa*) has passed, there occurs a single fire calamity that destroys the world-system.
What are its characteristics? According to the *Mūlasūtra*: "At the time of the three great calamities, a great black wind blows, causing the waters of the ocean to part on both sides;
it takes the sun palace and places it within the orbit of the sun upon the midpoint of Mount Sumeru. By means of this, the world-system [is destroyed]."
When two suns appear, the rivers and canals dry up. After a long period has passed, a great wind arises and takes away the third sun, whereby the Great Ganges dries up.
When the fourth sun appears, Lake Anavatapta dries up. When the fifth sun appears, the great ocean is parched and withered.

When the sixth sun appears, smoke rises from the great earth. When the seventh sun appears, the mountains and the earth blaze forth in flames. (The *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya Śāstra*, and the *Buddhanusmṛti Samādhi Sūtra* are all identical; the latter is largely the same.)
Everything from the Brahma Heaven down to the trichiliocosm was utterly consumed by fire; all the devas of the six heavens of desire reached the end of their lives.
Mount Sumeru collapsed, and a blazing conflagration reached as far as the Brahma Heaven.

The Brahma devas relinquished their lives and were reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, while everything below it was reduced to ashes and soot. The newly born devas had never before seen such a thing, and they were filled with universal apprehension.
The elder-born devas of the second dhyāna each come to console the newly born devas, saying, "Do not be afraid;

you shall never reach such a state" (meaning that while the calamity of fire destroys the first dhyāna, it does not reach the second dhyāna because there is no karma for fire therein; nevertheless, because the second dhyāna is adjacent to the first, the light from the destruction of the first dhyāna shines upon the second. When the newly born devas of the second dhyāna see this for the first time, they do not understand it and thus give rise to fear;
the elder devas, being accustomed to it, come to offer comfort). After the calamity of fire, when the kalpa is about to be formed, vast black clouds spread everywhere and rain falls profusely.
For countless thousands of years, drops as large as chariot axles fall until water fills the great trichiliocosm up to the Brahma-heaven;

this water gradually rises further until it reaches the Ābhāsvara Heaven (this is the water of the kalpa of formation). Then, as this water recedes, a great wind arises that stirs the waves and causes foam to gather;
this naturally solidifies and transforms into celestial palaces adorned with the seven treasures.

Here, the palaces of the Brahmā heavens diminish in water, and based on the previous mass of foam, the palaces of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens are successively formed, continuing down to the formation of the four continents, which are established as before.
(This clarifies the manner in which the world is re-formed: having been formed, it remains; having remained, it is destroyed.

Following this sequence, after seven calamities of fire have passed, the calamity of water finally arises. Regarding the second, the calamity of water: when beings in the lower realms are destroyed, they are all reborn in the third dhyāna heaven.

At that time, the calamity of boiling ash-water rains down like timely rain; from the palaces of the Ābhāsvara Heaven above, it follows the water and destroys everything until the lower heavens of the desire realm, leaving no forms behind.
Following the calamity of water, great clouds and rain arise once more to reconstruct the world, with the same process as the calamity of fire.

(In this sequence, after seven successive calamities of water, the calamity of wind finally arises. As for the three calamities of wind, it means that all sentient beings are born in the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the subsequent occurrence of the calamity of wind: after the calamity of water, after a long period of time, a great *saṃghāta* wind reaches the *Phala* Heaven (*Bṛhatphala*).
This wind spreads in the four directions, blowing against the celestial palaces of the various devas until they strike one another and shatter like fine dust.
This continues until it reaches the great mountain kings beneath the earth, which likewise strike one another; thus, the waters below the earth are completely exhausted.
When the wind has ceased, it subsequently sends down a great rain that reaches as far as the Fruit-Bearing Heaven (*Phala-deva*);
the wind stirs up waves and foam which accumulate as before, and the calamity of water re-establishes itself as it was.
The Diagram of the Three Calamities Spanning Kalpas:

The duration of time for the destruction of the kalpa by the three calamities is exceedingly vast and they do not arise simultaneously. That is to say, after one great kalpa, there occurs one fire calamity;
after seven such fire calamities, one encounters a water calamity; and after a long succession of these, only then does a wind calamity occur.
The beginning and end of the three great calamities (*mahākalpa*) together comprise sixty-four great kalpas as the count for one full cycle;
as a verse in the *Abhidharma-śāstra* says: "Seven fires follow in succession, and after..."
Then there is one water disaster, followed by seven fire disasters and seven water disasters;
after these, there are seven more fire disasters, followed by wind [disasters] (this is a summary of the sequence and number of the three calamities).
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "When these three great calamities of water, fire, and wind arise, they oppress sentient beings, causing them to abandon their lower realms."

Regarding the collection of the earth and the arising of calamities in the celestial realms: first, the calamity of fire arises due to the appearance of seven suns; next, the calamity of water arises due to the falling of torrential rains;

and finally, the calamity of wind arises due to the mutual clashing of winds. When these three calamities occur, what is their sequence? First, the calamities of fire must arise consecutively for seven times;
immediately following that, one calamity of water must necessarily arise; and after this, there must again be seven consecutive calamities of fire.
After seven calamities of fire, there is one calamity of water; this continues in such a manner until seven calamities of water have occurred.

Following this, there are seven more calamities of fire, after which a single calamity of wind arises. Thus, in total, there are eight cycles of seven calamities of fire, one cycle of seven calamities of water, and one calamity of wind.

The calamities of water and wind both follow immediately after the calamities of fire; this is because after a calamity of water or wind, a calamity of fire must necessarily arise. Therefore, there are three [types of] calamities.
The sequence of calamities is logically thus: for what reason do seven fires occur before one water calamity? It is because of the lifespan of the Ābhāsvara Heaven (i.e., the Light-Sound Heaven);
that is to say, their lifespan lasts for eight great kalpas, and it is only upon reaching the eighth [kalpa] that a single water calamity occurs.
From this, one should know that after passing through seven water calamities and eight sets of seven fire calamities, there is then one wind calamity, due to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
Regarding the power of longevity: because their lifespan lasts for sixty-four kalpas, there is one wind-disaster at the end of every eighth intermediate kalpa.

As sentient beings gradually excel in the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the karmic maturation (*vipāka*) they experience—namely, their physical bodies and lifespans—gradually increases. Consequently, the environments in which they dwell also become increasingly long-lasting.

(For example, as explained in detail regarding the Fourth Dhyāna, the lifespan in the Bṛhatphala heaven is five hundred kalpas; in the Ākāśānantyāyatana it is twenty thousand kalpas, up to eighty thousand kalpas in the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana. Their physical supports and enjoyments likewise gradually expand, and the duration of these kalpas is correspondingly long.)

Indeed, the power of karma is inconceivable and cannot be known by the world. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been bound by a continuous chain of karmic retribution through kalpas that are immeasurable and boundless; how could they be limited to merely ten million kalpas? Therefore, when the Buddha speaks of remote causes, he describes them in terms of the number of dust motes in a buddha-field.
Were it not for a Great Sage endowed with the six supernormal powers, who else could comprehend this?
The Schematics of the Arising of Buddhas Throughout the Three Great Kalpas:
Within these three great kalpas, three thousand Buddhas appear. The *Vibhūṣaṇa-kalpa* has already passed; the *Tārakā-kalpa* is yet to come;
and the *Bhadra-kalpa* is currently present, with one thousand Buddhas appearing to transform the world. Now, based on the *Bhadra-kalpa*, we shall briefly summarize it according to four periods.

This refers to the periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness. However, the kalpa of formation has already passed and the kalpas of destruction and emptiness have not yet arrived; we currently dwell in the kalpa of abiding.
Within this kalpa of abiding, there are twenty minor kalpas (*antarakalpa*), and it is during these twenty minor kalpas that Buddhas appear in succession.

In the Sahā world, since the beginning of the kalpa of entering [the cycle], eight cycles of decrease and eight cycles of increase (eight minor kalpas) have already passed without a Buddha appearing in the world.
Now, during the ninth cycle of decrease, four Buddhas will appear in the world: when the human lifespan decreases to sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appears;
next, when the human lifespan decreases to forty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appears.
When the human lifespan was decreasing from its peak to twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world;
when the human lifespan had decreased further to one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared in the world.

From the beginning of this *sthiti-kalpa* until the appearance of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, exactly fourteen billion two hundred seventy-nine million three thousand years have elapsed. Thus says the verse on the numerical reckoning of the Dharma.
It is said that during the *saṃbhava-kalpa* (the eon of formation) of this Sahā world, as the years flow on, there have been nine periods of decrease and eight periods of increase;
thus, [the total duration] is one hundred and four thousand, two hundred and seventy-nine million three thousand years.

Furthermore, from the parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored Śākyamuni until the Shaoxing era of the Song dynasty, two thousand one hundred years had already passed (according to a new calculation from the first year of the Shaoxing era of Emperor Gaozong of the Song dynasty until the Bingwu year of the Wanli era of our own dynasty, another four hundred and seventy-six years have elapsed). Moreover—
When twenty-one years have been subtracted [from the current era], the human body will have decreased by two chi and one cun;

at that time, people will be only six chi tall and live for eighty years. (The statement that the body will be eight chi when the lifespan reaches eighty is not necessarily so; this is because the length of the *chi* has varied between ancient and modern times. The Song *chi* was three chi and four cun longer than the Zhou *chi*;

one should take the Zhou *chi* as the standard, which would then correctly equal eight chi. From here, after another seven thousand years have passed, the human lifespan will be ten years and the body height will be one chi.
This marks the culmination of the kalpa of decrease (during which the three minor calamities occur). After this period, one enters the ninth kalpa of increase.
Starting from a human lifespan of ten years, as before, every hundred years the lifespan increases by one year and the body height increases by one inch.

Thus it gradually increases until the lifespan reaches eighty thousand years and a Cakravartin King of the Golden Wheel appears; this marks the culmination of the kalpa of increase. (Throughout the entire kalpa of increase...)

There will be four Wheel-Turning Kings who appear in the world. Subsequently, during the tenth *kalpa* of decrease, when the human lifespan has decreased to eighty thousand years, Maitreya Buddha will descend to be born.
From the time of the Xianheng era until the birth of Maitreya, eight million eight hundred and seventy thousand years will pass.
At that time, the ground of the ten billion Jambudvīpas will be made of pure gold, level as the palm of a hand; non-glutinous rice will grow spontaneously, and garments will appear upon thought.
When they come to desire food, food will appear, leading to immeasurable happiness. Men and women shall marry only after five hundred years.

At Maitreya’s first assembly, he will deliver ninety-two billion people; thereafter, he will deliver countless beings. The Buddha’s body will be thirty-two *zhang* tall, while the people will be sixteen *zhang* tall.
Maitreya will remain in the world for sixty thousand years, preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings before entering *nirvāṇa*.
The periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise be thus. In the *Sutra of the Wise and the Foolish*, the Buddha said: "Maitreya will deliver beings at three assemblies;
these are all those sentient beings who planted roots of merit through my bequeathed Dharma. Only then will he transform his followers who share the same affinity.

After Maitreya’s parinirvāṇa, [the lifespan] will gradually decrease until human life reaches ten years. This marks the end of the tenth *kṣaya-kalpa* (decreasing eon), after which one enters the tenth *vardhana-kalpa* (increasing eon). This constitutes the eleventh eon."
For fourteen kalpas no Buddha appeared in the world. During the fifteenth kalpa, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas arose in the world.
From the sixteenth to the nineteenth kalpa, likewise, no Buddha appeared.
Then, in the twentieth kalpa, the final Buddha, Ruci (Louti), appeared to transform the world; after his parinirvāṇa, one thousand Buddhas appeared, completing the twenty *ulūka* (revolving) kalpas.

Once they are full, the period of destruction arrives (encountering the three great calamities); after a long time, they are formed again, creating the heavens and earth of the future *nakṣatra-kalpa*.
Since there are also one thousand Buddhas who appear in the world, the verse summarizing the three thousand Buddhas says:
The Buddhas of the past thousand eons, citing the first and last: Śobhita, Padmaprabha, and Viśvabhū; The Buddhas of the present Bhadrakalpa, citing the first and last: Krakucchanda and Ruci;

The Buddhas of the future thousand eons, citing the first and last: Jyotīrasa, Sūryaprabha, and Merudhvaja. Such are the Buddhas who deliver sentient beings throughout the reckoning of kalpas and years.
According to the *Zhuangchun ji*, the number of years constituting a kalpa is calculated as follows:
one small kalpa (also called a "separate kalpa" or a "pulley kalpa") refers to one cycle of decrease and increase.

Calculating the total of these increases and decreases amounts to 1,680,000 years (as previously calculated: starting from eighty-four thousand years, subtracting one year for every hundred years passed until reaching ten years, which takes eighty-four thousand years).

One thousand sets of one hundred years constitute eight million four hundred thousand years; because the years accumulated during the periods of increase and decrease are combined, they total sixteen million eight hundred thousand years, which is called one *kalpa* (a cycle).
Twenty such cycles of increase and decrease are likewise calculated.
The two intermediate kalpas (referring to the four periods such as the kalpa of abiding) consist of twenty *ulūka-kalpas*.

Taken together, these twenty cycles of increase and decrease total thirty-three million six hundred thousand years (which is also twenty times one million six hundred and eighty thousand years), and this is termed one *sthiti-kalpa* (an intermediate kalpa of abiding).
The three kalpas of destruction, emptiness, and formation are likewise calculated in the same manner.

The three great kalpas refer to the four intermediate kalpas. Taken together, these four intermediate kalpas—equivalent to eighty minor kalpas—total one million three hundred forty-four thousand years (which is also four times thirty-three million six hundred thousand years); this is termed a single great kalpa.
This constitutes the ultimate limit of the formation and destruction of heaven and earth; as they cycle again and begin anew, their movement is infinite.
Contemplate this: because empty space is immeasurable, the worlds are boundless; because the Great Transformation is infinite, the cycles of kalpas have no end.
Within this Great Transformation, a great kalpa is like a single year; its phases of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness are the four seasons;
its eighty increments and decrements are the twenty-four solar energies (*qi*); and the Four Wheel-Turning Kings are like the *qilin* of early summer.
The Phoenix is like a human amidst the three calamities, while the latter is like an autumn insect in the midst of a severe frost.
How much more so these trivial, sentient beings who bustle about, coming and going, no different from mosquitoes and gnats in a vessel, clamoring and frolicking in confusion.

Born once through transformation and dying again through transformation, drifting and tossing upon the ocean of change—where ultimately do they go? It is but a dream within a dream; in the long, dark night, they grasp at the void.
If, in truth, there had never been one who awakened to the Sun [of Wisdom], and no Great Awakened One or Great Sage had appeared in the world, who then would have awakened others?
Someone asked: "According to Shao Yong’s *Jingshi*, the number of years for the waxing and waning of a single *yuan* is 1,296,000;
this constitutes the ultimate limit of the beginning and end of Heaven and Earth. Compared with the preceding *mahākalpa*..."
If it is but one ten-thousandth part, how can the disparity between the two be so great? Yet, there cannot be two truths in the world; which, then, is correct? The answer is:
the great numbers regarding the formation and destruction of heaven and earth can only be known and seen by those who are sages and possess the six supernatural powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*);
how could they be fathomed by the limited wisdom of worldly people? Worldly persons may only speak of mundane affairs; once these have passed, [they are beyond their reach].
If one asks whether the "number of the single primal unity" (*yīyuán zhī shù*) is not a supramundane teaching, I say: No; it is the principle of the *Yī* (Book of Changes).
While the principle of Shao Yong’s number of the single primal unity is indeed thus, his statement regarding "opening things and closing things" is a metaphorical analogy.

It is like the operation of a single year, which has its periods of decline (*fǒu*) and prosperity (*tài*); if one traces this back through successive stages, it culminates in what is unified by the single primal unity.
Within the span of one hundred and twenty-nine thousand six hundred years, there are likewise periods of prosperity (*tai*) and decline (*pi*).

Since the movement of the *qi* corresponds to the years, it is said that "things are opened in the month of Yin and things are closed in the month of Xu. This may well be the principle: that in the month of Jingzhi (Awakening from Hibernation), things are brought forth, while in the month of Shuangjiang (Frost’s Descent), things are brought to an end.
This holds true if one considers it as the numerical cycle of the great movement of prosperity and decline; however, if one considers the formation of Heaven and Earth...
That the destruction [of the world] occurs according to those specific numbers is not necessarily so.

If it were indeed according to those numbers, then when the human population reaches the eighth assembly at the *yin* stage, and after the ninth assembly at the *xu* stage, all humans would cease to exist and heaven and earth would follow suit and perish.

If heaven and earth were indeed destroyed after the *xu* stage, where would Maitreya Buddha and the others be born? (According to what was previously seen, there are one thousand Buddhas within the currently existing heaven and earth.)
If the world beyond has already perished and there is no ground upon which beings can be born, was there no one before the previous kalpa? If there were no people, who was the Wheel-Turning King?
If people were born after that period, then the Wheel-Turning King should still exist (for the lifespan of a Wheel-Turning King is eighty thousand years).

Thus, while numbers may indeed experience waxing and waning (as in the aforementioned kalpas of increase and decrease), how could the heavens and earth depend on human calculations, and could they too be destroyed by them?
The Chart of the Established Order of the Dharma Realm, Middle Volume, Part Two;
and the Chart of the Established Order of the Dharma Realm, Lower Volume, Part One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Renchao of Yanshan.

Five: Traveling to the Buddha-fields of the Ten Directions, Illustration of the Buddha-fields of the Ten Directions (Explanatory Text), Illustration of the Pure Land of the East, Illustration of the Pure Land of the West (Text, Part 11): The Ground Adorned with the Seven Jewels.
Palaces of the seven treasures, lotus bathing pools, rows of trees, and the sounds of music;
jeweled nets radiating light, crest-light shining afar, and transformed birds expounding the Dharma;
long lifespans, the primary cause for rebirth, and the manifestation of punishment within the City of Doubt.

The Pure Land’s Primary Retribution: A General Exposition of the Diagram of One Floating Banner Buddha-field, the Diagram of Ten Floating Banner Buddha-fields, and the Diagram of a Hundred Floating Banner Buddha-fields;
An Explanation of the Karmic Causes of the Flower Treasury World; and the Interpretation of the Name "Flower Treasury."
The general title, "Wandering through the Buddha-fields," refers to the profound mind of faith and understanding that universally observes the divine wisdom of all Buddha-lands.
Indeed, those who recognize the existence of humans and devas but do not know of the Buddhas are merely worldly commoners; it is by believing in the Buddha that one transcends them.
The Great Sages of the world are vessels for the Path; yet, while the merit of believing in a single Buddha is superior, its scope of vision remains limited.
If one believes in many Buddhas, the measure of that merit becomes boundless, and the scope of that wisdom increases accordingly.

The Buddha-fields of the ten directions take the trichiliocosm as a single Buddha-field. Thus, beyond this Sahā world, within the great void of space, there are further Buddha-fields of the trichiliocosm in the ten directions.
How is this known? According to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, regarding this Sahā world:
To the east of this world, there is another world named Guhyaviniścaya; to the south, a world named Abhyudgata;
to the west, a world named Vimala; to the north, a world named Saṃpatti; to the northeast, a world named Parigraha;
to the southeast, a world named Upakāra; and to the southwest, a world named...
To the northwest of the world Freshness (Xian-shao-ci), there is a world named Joyful (Huan-xi-ci); below it is a world named Lock-and-Key (Guān-yuè-ci);
and above it is a world named Resounding Sound (Zhen-yin-ci).

In each of these worlds of the ten directions, the Tathāgatas each have one hundred billion names, so that all sentient beings may individually know and see them; this extends even to the countless worlds of the ten directions.

Furthermore, it is thus: (In one set of four continents, a Buddha has ten thousand names; since there are ten billion sets of four continents in a trichiliocosm, there are ten billion times ten million names. The same applies to the trichiliocosms throughout the ten directions.)

The *Sūtra on the Merits of the Seven Buddhas of the Pure Land of the East* states: "To the east, passing beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of four Gaṅgā rivers, there is a world named Invincible (*Anabhibhūta*), where the Buddha is named King of Auspiciousness and Good Renown (*Kīrtiśrī-rāja*) Tathāgata; this land is likewise adorned with jewels."
Next, to the east of the Lotus-Earth Transformation-Birth [Buddha-field], passing through five *gaṅgā* sands of Buddha-fields, there is a world named Wondrous Jewel;
the Buddha there is named Ratnacandravimalaprabhāsvaramaheśvararāja Tathāgata.
Next, to the east, passing through six *gaṅgā* sands of Buddha-fields, there is a world named Perfect Fragrance-Accumulation; the Buddha there is named Golden Jewel Light.
To the east of the Tathāgata King Accomplished in Sublime Conduct, passing through seven *gaṅgā* sands of buddha-fields, there is a world named Aśoka;
the Buddha there is named Aśoka-uttama-śrī-rāja Tathāgata.
To the east of that, passing through eight *gaṅgā* sands of buddha-fields, there is a world named Dharmadhvaja; the Buddha there is named Dharmasāgara-nirghoṣa-rāja Tathāgata.
Proceeding eastward from here, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as nine *gaṅgā* sands, there is a world named Sthitaprabhāsa-ratnasāgara;
the Buddha there is named Dharmasāgaravijayamati-vikrīḍita-abhijñārāja Tathāgata.
Proceeding eastward from here, passing through Buddha-lands as numerous as ten *gaṅgā* sands, there is a world named Vimala-vaidūrya; the Buddha there is named Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabharāja.
All these Buddha-worlds that have come forth are equal in their adornment of merit to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, without any difference.

(The Gaṅgā, or Ganges, is a river forty li wide with sand as fine as flour; one grain of sand is calculated as one Buddha-field, and the total number of Buddha-fields in the entire river is called "one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [Ganges-sand] Buddha-field").
The Diagram of the Western Pure Land:
Why is the Western Pure Land called a "Pure Land"? Because the world is bright and pure, it is termed "pure"; that which is inhabited by this purity is termed "land."
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that the land inhabited is free from the five turbidities and is like crystal and other such substances, thus it is called a "Pure Land.
The *Abhidharmakośa* states that the dwelling place of sentient beings who are free from afflictions is called a "Pure Land.
Although the lands of the ten directions are indeed pure, the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is the most preeminent of all.

The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "From here, to the west, passing through a hundred thousand myriads of koṭis of buddha-fields (a million according to the *Mahāvaipulya* version), there is a world named Sukhāvatī.
For what reason is that land called 'Supreme Bliss' (*Sukhāvatī*)?

Because the sentient beings in that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is therefore named 'Supreme Bliss. (The *Mahāvaipulya* version says: 'There are sounds of spontaneous purity and matters of spontaneous happiness. "
Regarding the adornment of the ground with the seven treasures, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states:

"Within the land of Amitābha Buddha, all things are spontaneously composed of the seven treasures—namely, gold, silver, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, amber, and musaragalva. Their essential nature is soft and gentle because of this."
The ground is interspersed with the seven treasures, its radiant colors shining with marvelous purity. (The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "Upon the ground of lapis lazuli, golden cords are interlaced;
demarcated by the boundaries of the seven treasures, they clearly distinguish the divisions, emitting various kinds of light. This light is like flowers, or like stars and the moon.

It is vast and level, devoid of Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, the great oceans, or pits, ravines, and wells. There are also no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras—there is only the self.
Furthermore, the flowing springs are free from cold or heat (the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* [Xiaoben] says they are free from the three evil realms).

The palaces and halls of those seven treasures, as well as the lecture hall and vihara of that Buddha, are composed of the seven treasures; there are also jeweled towers, pavilions, and railings (the *Xiaoben* mentions sevenfold railings).
Adorned with exquisite and wondrous necklaces of precious jewels, their pure radiance is peerless; the palatial dwellings where these bodhisattvas and śrāvakas reside are likewise so.
The palaces and towers inhabited by devas and worldly beings vary in height and size according to their forms, being composed of one, two, or even many kinds of jewels;
some are situated beneath the earth, while others hang suspended in mid-air. As they follow [the conditions of] form, they are...

According to the thickness or thinness of their merit, each receives their respective enjoyment (in the *Amitābha Sūtra*, it is said that in every realm of the land of various jewels there are five hundred billion jeweled towers; the *Shorter Version* states they are "pavilions adorned with the four jewels").

In the Lotus Bathing Pond there are various pools and marshes; some are made of gold, some of silver, some of crystal and lapis lazuli, some of coral and amber, and even some made of the seven precious gems;
the sands on their bottoms are likewise composed of these same materials.
In those jewel ponds, there are some forty *li* square, others fifty-six, and so on up to twenty thousand four hundred and eighty *li* square;
some are like the great ocean, and some are bathing pools for the Buddha.
These are composed of various jewels and filled to the brim with water of eight virtues—profound, pure, fragrant, clean, and sweet as nectar—in a hundred varieties.
Various flowers emit a rich and fragrant scent. Within each of the ponds made of the seven treasures, there are sixty billion lotus flowers made of the seven treasures.
Each lotus flower is twelve *yojanas* in size, and each precious flower has hundreds of thousands of millions of petals.
The radiance of these flowers is immeasurable and of various colors: blue with blue light, white with white light, and colors such as dark purple, yellow, vermilion, and magenta.
The light was likewise brilliant, radiant, and dazzling, outshining the sun and moon; its flowing radiance manifested transformation-buddhas who preached the Dharma of purity.
Amidst the music of the trees and the banks of various jewel-pools stood countless sandalwood trees and auspicious fruit trees, their flowers and fruits perpetually fragrant.

The fragrant scent wafted abroad; furthermore, there were seven kinds of jewel-trees—some made of a single jewel, some of two jewels, up to those made of all seven jewels as a single tree—with roots, trunks, branches, and leaves each consisting of a different jewel.
Such trees were planted in rows, their trunks facing one another, arranged in hundreds of thousands of layers (seven layers in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*), pervading the world in its entirety.
The wind blows upon them, producing exquisite and delightful sounds that all proclaim the sublime Dharma.

Jeweled nets radiate light, and furthermore, immeasurable jeweled nets completely cover that buddha-field; they are composed entirely of gold, silver, pearls, and hundreds of thousands of various precious gems.
Adorned and embellished with wondrous, rare, and precious ornaments, they were draped all around and radiated brilliant light;
when gentle breezes blew upon the nets, they produced the sounds of the sublime Dharma, or they blew exquisite flowers that were scattered everywhere.

The light from the crown of his head shines afar, reaching all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions. Those who are reborn in that land are all born by transformation within lotus flowers in jeweled ponds;
they grow naturally without needing to be nursed at a breast, partaking of spontaneous food, their bodies entirely golden in color and their features perfectly handsome.

This is truly beyond worldly comparison; it is simply that the light varies in magnitude: the radiance from the Buddha’s crown illuminates thousands of millions of worlds (the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* states:

"His light is immeasurable, illuminating the lands of the ten directions"), while the radiance from a Bodhisattva’s crown illuminates thousands of billions of *li*, and the radiance from a Śrāvaka’s crown each illuminates seven *zhang*.
Transformed birds that expound the Dharma—white cranes, peacocks, parrots, śārikas, kalaviṅkas, and saṃjīvaka birds—all likewise proclaim the sounds of the Dharma;

these are all transformations produced by the Buddha’s spiritual power (the "Small Text" reads: "All these various birds are created through the transformations of Amitābha Buddha, who desires to cause his harmonious Dharma-sounds to flow forth").
His lifespan is long and far-reaching;

because the lifespan of that Buddha and that of his people lasts for immeasurable, boundless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, he is named Amitābha (*asaṃkhyeya* here means "innumerable," which is a name for a great kalpa).
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One kalpa in the Sahā world is [the duration of] one day and night in Sukhāvatī."
The world constitutes one day and night.

For those who truly desire to be reborn there with the correct cause for rebirth, there are three grades. The highest grade consists of those who leave their homes, renounce desire, and become śramaṇas with a sincere mind.

One who is free from covetousness, upholds the sutras and precepts, practices the six *pāramitās*, performs the deeds of a bodhisattva, and single-mindedly contemplates that Buddha while cultivating all manner of merit, will see the Buddha and bodhisattvas in a dream.
At the end of their life, the Buddha and his assembly of sages will come to welcome them;
they will be born by transformation within that jewel pond and become one among the bodhisattvas, even if they cannot become a śramaṇa.
Extensively cultivating merit, always believing and accepting the Buddha’s words, deeply generating the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta, single-mindedly recollecting that Buddha,

practicing goodness according to one's ability, upholding the fasts and precepts, erecting stupas and images, providing food for śramaṇas, hoisting banners, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense—
dedicating these merits with the vow to be born in that land, at the end of life, a transformation Buddha will come to welcome and lead one there.
Regarding the merit of being born in that place: those whose merit is next below the former cannot perform various meritorious deeds or resolve their minds upon the Great Way;
they simply maintain single-minded recollection of the Buddha ten times every day. At the end of life, they dream of the Buddha and also attain rebirth there;

their merit is next to the intermediate level. Furthermore, there are three grades; the next [grade] consists of those who observe the fasts and precepts with purity and recite the Buddha’s name with a single mind for ten days.

If one does not cease [the recitation] during the night, at the end of life one will certainly attain rebirth there. Furthermore, even if one cannot do so for ten days and nights, one should eliminate all distracting thoughts and cast away sorrow;
one must not approach women, but keep the body upright and the mind correct, severing craving and desire while maintaining the purity of the fast and precepts.
By recollecting the Buddha’s name without ceasing for a single day and night, one will likewise attain rebirth there. Moreover, if men or women resolve to attain Bodhi—

Upholding the various precepts in one's mind, performing virtuous deeds to benefit sentient beings, and maintaining mindfulness of that Buddha and his buddha-field, one will be welcomed by the Buddha at the end of life and be reborn through transformation in the Pure Land.

(It is also said: "One must surely cultivate the ten wholesome paths in order to be born in that buddha-field. The *Shorter Text* states: "Whether for one day, two days, or up to seven days, if one maintains single-mindedness without distraction, one shall immediately attain rebirth.")
The City of Doubt Manifests as Punishment:

If a person cultivates merit with the aspiration to be born in that land, but later develops a regretful mind, harboring doubt and lack of faith regarding that Buddha-land and those who have been reborn there;
if they continue to have thoughts of it yet momentarily believe and then disbelieve, their will wavering and hesitant, and they subsequently repent—[they shall be reborn in the City of Doubt].
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha will also be born in that land, within the cities of the seven treasures in the border regions, by transformation from a lotus flower;

their food and clothing will appear spontaneously, and they will experience celestial bliss. However, for five hundred years within those cities, they will not see the Buddha-dharma or bodhisattvas, which constitutes their suffering.
This is shown as a minor retribution; therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha should believe with deep sincerity and make a vow.
When seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, do not harbor doubts that lead to such karmic retribution.

Regarding the primary retribution, the *Lianzong baojian* states in general terms: "Because one cultivates pure karma, the fruit is the attainment of the Pure Land; the Transformation Buddha leads one upward to the Golden Terrace. This is the stage of the Sages.

The Sage welcomes them back to the Land of Bliss, transcending the three realms and surging beyond the four currents. Karmic deeds are exhausted and defilements vanish; worldly emotions cease and discursive thoughts are severed.

Their physical substance rests within the calyx of a lotus, while their spirit wanders through the midst of the precious realm. There they personally attend upon Amitābha as their primary teacher, and behold Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta as their close friends.
Amidst the great assembly of the pure ocean of beings, they dwell within the precious pond of the nine grades of excellence.

The streams each recounted his past deeds: five fragrances brushed his body, and the three virtues adorned his person. A gentle breeze briefly fanned him as he listened to the various sounds of the Dharma being proclaimed;
amidst a profusion of falling flower-rain, he beheld the radiance of the spreading net of flames. Floating amidst ethereal clouds and mists, his divine feet moved with lightness and ease;

his robes were filled with the reception of wondrous flowers. In the morning, he paid homage at the Compassionate One’s countenance, and having received the seal of the Dharma, he returned to his kingdom at dusk.
Wandering through the golden lands and listening to the jade-like verses, one attains carefree ease; as auspicious lotuses first bloom, residual calamities are dispelled.

For those newly born through transformation, their practice becomes non-regressive; how could it be that they merely forget coarse suffering for the time being? Nay, the fruit of Buddhahood is not far off. One sports amidst the jade groves and bathes in the waters of virtue;
the pavilions of a hundred jewels are magnificent and resplendent, and the sevenfold rows of trees stand solemn and majestic. The scenery is sublime.

The land of Eternal Spring is as level as the palm of a hand; food and clothing arrive according to one's thoughts. Celestial music resounds spontaneously without being struck, and enjoyments arise naturally.
This bliss is truly not of this human world; even ten billion times the heavens cannot compare to it.
All Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, praise it; their bodies possess radiant and wondrous marks, and their feet tread upon the fragrant path of the sages.
Their stages of life are immeasurable and their compassionate vows are inexhaustible. Having relinquished the two types of birth, they are no longer subject to the cycle of birth and death;
having attained the eternal radiance of the ultimate limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), they are free from the marks of coming and going.

That their conditions are powerful, their virtues supreme, and that all their merit is complete and their lifespan long—all these are the results of the pure causes induced by the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha. Thus we know that the Buddha possesses the vow to gather in sentient beings, and that sentient beings possess [the capacity for] birth.
The causes for perceiving the Buddha are such that these supreme conditions arise from faith and aspiration; by means of this wondrous fruit, one achieves the true reliance.

Whether sitting in meditation or reciting sutras by the banks of the Seven Treasures Pond, or walking in meditation upon the golden ground, one is satiated with the precious flavors of dhyāna-joy and Dharma-delight.
Wearing the celestial robes of compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity, one’s merit nourishes the spirit, increasing both pity and wisdom as one gracefully accomplishes the Way.
Nurturing the noble embryo, they enter the gate of non-arising and ascend to the rank of Bodhisattva; attaining the state of *avaivartika*, they do not regress from the mind of enlightenment.

Abiding in the family of the Dharma-king, they receive the predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) of all Tathāgatas; hearing the Mahāyāna Dharma, they are equally honored as those in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Moment by moment they dwell in the profound and void, heart and mind in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); they attain the right samādhi and possess the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣadabhijñā*).
With supernormal powers, he makes offerings throughout the ten directions, coming and going without obstruction; he manifests emanations in billions of lands without losing his concentrated mind.

He sprinkles the water of the Dharma upon the three thousandfold world-system and rescues sentient beings from the burning house. Benefiting both self and others, his practices and vows are perfected;
it may be said that the hundreds of thousands of samādhis, all being the merit of the mind-only adorned, have returned to his own self.
If one views this Land of Ultimate Bliss from the perspective of the Sahā world, it lies ten trillion Buddha-fields to the west;
yet if one views it from the perspective of the world-systems (*lokadhātu-vīja*), the Land of Ultimate Bliss is still within the thirteenth layer,
not far from the intermediate Sahā world, for to the west of the Sahā world there are worlds as numerous as the atoms of a Buddha-field.
Extending from the realms and so forth to the thirteenth layer at the extreme western limit, this Ultimate Bliss is the place where those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha are reborn;
it truly exists as a pure land of the seven treasures. To maintain that there is no pure land is a statement of false view.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the chapter on the Diagram of the Floating Banner Buddha-field, states:

"There are as many fragrant water oceans as there are atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of buddha-fields, situated within the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean, distributed like the net of Indra; this is the central fragrant water ocean."
It is named Boundless Light of Wondrous Flowers, and it rests upon a world-system called Adorned with All-Fragrant Mani-King Jewels,
which has as its base a mani-king banner that manifests the forms of all bodhisattvas. From this world-system emerges a great lotus flower named Adorned with All-Fragrant Mani-Kings,
and upon it dwells a world named Blazing Jewel Radiance Illuminating the Ten Directions, which has all manner of ornaments as its substance and possesses ten [thousand worlds].
Within worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakable Buddha-fields, arrayed one after another,
there is a world at the very bottom named Most Victorious Light Pervading Illumination. It is surrounded by worlds as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field,
and above this, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a Buddha-field, there is a world named Kind.
Surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in two Buddha-fields, the Buddha named Kindly Fragrant Lotus Wondrous Adornment is called Lion Light Supreme Illumination.
Above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a Buddha-field, is a world named Universal Radiance of All Jewel Adornments;
its Buddha is named Pure Light Wisdom Supreme Banner, and [it is surrounded] by as many [worlds] as there are atoms in three Buddha-fields.

Surrounded on all sides by a multitude of worlds numbering as many as the atoms in a world-system, above this, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Various Radiant Flower Adornments;
its Buddha is named Vajra Radiance of Infinite Diligence and Power, surrounded on all sides by worlds numbering as many as the atoms in four buddha-fields.
Above this, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field...
In this realm, there is a world named Universal Radiance of Exquisite Flower Light,
surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in five buddha-fields; above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field,
there is a world named Pure and Wondrous Radiance, where the Buddha is named Universal Light Spontaneous Banner, and it is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in six buddha-fields.
Surrounding this world on all sides, beyond worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Array of Multitude Flower Flames;
its Buddha is named Ocean of Joy, Merit, and Renown of Self-Righteous Radiance.
Surrounding that world on all sides are worlds as numerous as the atoms in seven buddha-fields. Beyond those, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there is...
The world-system is named Birth of the Ground of Sovereign Power, and its Buddha is named Banner of the Ocean of Wisdom with Vast Renown.
It is surrounded on all sides by as many world-systems as there are atoms in eight buddha-fields.
Above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, is a world named Emanation of Wondrous Sounds; its Buddha is named Mark of Pure Moonlight Radiance, Unconquerable. Nine.

Surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, beyond these worlds there is a world named Vajradhvaja, which is surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
beyond this, there is a world as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field... [where] the Buddha is named Sarvadharmasāgaravara-rāja.
The world is named Constantly Manifesting Sapphire Radiance, and the Buddha’s name is Immeasurable Merit Dharma;
it is surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in eleven buddha-fields.

Above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Radiant Illumination, and the Buddha’s name is Surpassing Śakra and Brahmā; [it is surrounded] by as many [worlds] as there are atoms in twelve buddha-fields.
Surrounded on all sides by a multitude of worlds numbering as many as the atoms in a world-system, above this lies a world named Sahā.
Its Buddha is Vairocana, and it is surrounded on all sides by worlds numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen buddha-fields.
(The World of Ultimate Bliss is situated within these surrounding satellite worlds. Above this, past worlds numbering as many as the atoms in a buddha-field...
There is a world named Tranquil Light Free from Dust, surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in fourteen buddha-fields;

above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, is a world named Lamp of Many Sublime Radiances, where the Buddha is named Banner of Universal Illumination with Invincible Power. Fifteenth.

Surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, above this, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Pure Light Pervasive Illumination; its Buddha is named Pure Sun Virtue Eye.
It is surrounded on all sides by worlds as numerous as the atoms in sixteen buddha-fields. Above this, past worlds as numerous as the atoms in a buddha-field...
In this realm, there is a world named Illuminating the Ten Directions, surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in seventeen buddha-fields;
above this, past as many worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Free from Dust,
where the Buddha is named Supreme Banner of Infinite Expedient Means, and it is surrounded by as many worlds as there are atoms in eighteen buddha-fields.

Surrounded on all sides by a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a buddha-field, above this, past a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world named Pure Light Universally Illuminating;
its Buddha is named Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu and Space-Light.
Surrounded on all sides by a number of worlds equal to the atoms in nineteen buddha-fields, above this, past a number of worlds equal to the atoms in a buddha-field, there is a world...
The realm is named Wondrous Jewel Flame, and it is surrounded on all sides by as many worlds as there are atoms in twenty buddha-fields.
Within this world-system of Blazing Jewel Light Illumining the Ten Directions, there are such unspeakable numbers [of worlds].
There are as many vast worlds as there are atoms in a buddha-field, each with its own basis of support, its own shape, its own essential nature,
its own orientation, its own mode of entry, its own adornment, its own boundaries,
its own arrangement, its own lack of differentiation, and its own power of empowerment, all surrounding and adorning one another— namely, the ten Buddhas.
Worlds shaped like the revolutions of atoms of buddha-fields; worlds shaped like rivers as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields;
worlds shaped like swirling currents as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields; worlds shaped like wheel-rims as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields;
worlds shaped like sacrificial altars as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields; and worlds shaped like trees as numerous as the atoms of ten buddha-fields.
Worlds shaped like forests, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; worlds shaped like multi-storied pavilions, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
worlds shaped like banners of ethical discipline (*śīla*), as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; worlds shaped like universal squares, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
worlds shaped like wombs (*garbha*), as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; and worlds shaped like lotuses.
Worlds in the shape of *kharaka* fruits, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; worlds in the shape of sentient beings, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
worlds in the shape of the marks of a Buddha, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; worlds in the shape of circular halos, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields;
worlds in the shape of clouds, as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields; [and worlds] as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields...
There are worlds shaped like nets numbering as many as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, and worlds shaped like gate-towers numbering likewise;
such worlds are as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably many buddha-fields.

Each of these individual worlds is surrounded by a perimeter of ten times the number of atoms in a buddha-field of vast worlds. Within each of these worlds, there are again [arrays] as described above.
It is said that worlds as numerous as atoms constitute its retinue;
all these worlds thus described are contained within this Boundless Exquisite Flower Light Fragrant Water Ocean and within the fragrant rivers that surround this ocean.
The *Qingliang shu* states: "According to the introductory and concluding sections, there are [in total] as many worlds as atoms in unspeakably many Buddha-fields;
however, in the detailed enumeration, only nineteen Buddha-field atoms are listed as twenty tiers. The number of fields that can surround [the central one] is merely two hundred and ten field-atoms.

(The commentary clarifies that while the introduction and conclusion indicate a great number, the specific enumeration is fewer; the supplementary note explains that the sutra takes twenty worlds as the primary units along with their retinues.)

If there were twenty tiers, would it not be the case that the buddha-fields passed through in the intermediate spaces lacked retinues? If so, how could the eight directions and the zenith and nadir be established as being filled in successive layers without gaps? Therefore, one knows this is not the case; thus the text concludes by stating, "There are such numbers as these.

From this, we know that the eight directions are filled layer upon layer in equal measure, without difference, and that their number is complete.
